Vizio and Samsung TVs both appeared to send this data even when researchers opted out of ACR. Only four out of eight smart TVs appeared to completely honor ACR opt-out. If you thought that opting out of surveillance on your smart TV would give you your privacy back, think again. A study by researchers at Northeastern University found that some smart TVs still seem to send information about what you’re watching to third parties, even after you pressed the opt-out button. The study, ‘ Watching the watchers ‘, tested twelve smart TVs from ten manufacturers to find out how well they respected opt-outs from automatic content recognition (ACR). ACR is a TV feature that captures audio and/or video content from smart TVs and uploads it to a third party (typically the TV manufacturer). The third party converts this content into digital fingerprints to understand what you’re watching, and can then use it to send targeted advertising or allow others to do the same. It’s on most if not all smart TVs, and 82% of US households had a smart TV as of last year. The test took in the eight operating systems behind roughly 95% of US smart TVs, and ran ten viewing scenarios on each of them. These ranged from viewing antenna TV through to viewing via screen mirroring from another device. items.title: New York's Queens Public Library battles ransomware crims: Wi-Fi, checkouts, and website go dark
items.summary: No gang has claimed the attack on incredible neighborhood resource yet
items.raw: New York City's Queens Public Library (QPL) is battling a ransomware attack, it confirmed on Wednesday evening via social media and to patrons directly. The disruption has downed QPL's website, on-site computers, check-out and return machines, its public Wi-Fi, mobile app, and its digital media services. Renewals are also unavailable, although library users are not charged fines for returning materials late. (Since 2021, In October 2021, QPL, Brooklyn Public Library, and New York Public Library - in an effort to help lower income users from being put off borrowing - permanently killed daily late fines on books and circulating materials.) Each of the library system's 66 locations remains open, including the central library in the Jamaica neighborhood in Queens, but QPL warned: "it will take some time before the library's network and systems are restored." QPL said "certain virtual and in-person programs may be impacted," advising visitors to check availability with their local branch via phone, and check the library's social media channels for official updates. "Our IT department is working to resolve the issue, and we will keep you informed,” it said in the statement. It added: "We apologize for any inconvenience and appreciate your patience." No established ransomware group has yet claimed responsibility for the disruption, although attacks on publicly funded institutions rarely lead to lucrative payouts. The British Library's infamous ransomware attack in 2023 at the hands of Rhysida saw the organization refuse to pay the criminals' 20 Bitcoin ransom demand, opting instead to drain its cash reserves and fork out millions for an IT rebuild. Although the library's response to the attack drew widespread praise, few institutions of its kind are in a financial position to follow its lead. Other libraries might not be willing or able to commit to a recovery period as lengthy as that of the British Library. In its 2025/26 annual report, published in July, the institution said its recovery is still incomplete, and work to fully restore customers' ability to purchase electronic resources, such as journals and research databases, and reopen access to electronic legal deposit content is ongoing. This is likely to be completed by the end of 2026, the British Library added. ®

items.title: PEC da Segurança Pública: o que muda para a tecnologia das polícias?
items.summary: A PEC da Segurança Pública incorpora a existência do Susp à Constituição Federal.
items.raw: O Senado Federal aprovou nesta terça-feira (3) a PEC da Segurança Pública (PEC 18/2025) . A proposta revisa a atuação das forças de segurança nacionais, prevê medidas mais rigorosas contra o crime organizado e incorpora à Constituição Federal o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (Susp), responsável por promover a integração entre os órgãos de segurança. No campo da tecnologia, a PEC reforça diretrizes de interoperabilidade entre sistemas policiais, compartilhamento de informações e provas e desenvolvimento de soluções tecnológicas para a segurança pública . Algumas dessas medidas já existiam na legislação, mas passam a ter respaldo constitucional. O combate aos crimes cibernéticos também não é tratado diretamente pela proposta . A PEC não cria novos tipos penais para ataques a sistemas, invasão de dispositivos ou fraudes digitais, mas amplia as competências da Polícia Federal para atuar em determinados crimes de repercussão interestadual ou internacional, o que pode incluir delitos praticados pela internet. Além disso, a PEC não determina a implementação de ferramentas específicas de inteligência artificial , reconhecimento facial ou monitoramento digital. A adoção dessas tecnologias dependerá das normas aplicáveis e das decisões dos órgãos responsáveis pela segurança pública. Embora reforce a importância da tecnologia para a segurança pública, a PEC 18/2025 não determina a implementação imediata de novas ferramentas ou plataformas digitais. Em vez disso, ela estabelece diretrizes constitucionais para a integração entre os órgãos de segurança, reservando as decisões sobre tecnologias e os detalhes sobre seu funcionamento à legislação e às decisões de órgãos responsáveis. Para continuar acompanhando as novidades sobre tecnologia, segurança digital e políticas públicas, fique ligado no TecMundo .

Norway's aid agency pwned and all users' data is stolen
items.summary: Norad said it cannot be sure that the details of those in 'conflict areas and authoritarian states' are safe or not
items.raw: Norway's national aid agency, Norad, has confirmed that cyber criminals broke into its systems, stealing information about each and every registered user of its grant portal. Norad, which coordinates Norway's assistance for foreign development, said that 20,614 registered individuals had their names and email addresses swiped, and information from at least three organizations' applications was "misdirected." The agency clarified that the grant portal, which was launched in 2017, has 20,614 registered users, meaning all were affected, across 12,511 organizations. In addition, the grant applications for at least three organizations are confirmed to be involved, though Norad said it may discover more as its investigation continues. Torger Kjeldstad, director of digitalization at Norad, said "the attack is complex," and confirmed the agency has initiated a crisis team to manage it. "We know a lot about what has happened, but to ensure that we have a complete overview of the attack, we are working to engage external experts in cybersecurity," he said. "They will give us a detailed description of what information those who attacked the solution have gained access to." Kjeldstad added that "it should be safe" to continue using Norad's services while it continues to probe what happened, and who was behind it. Norad did not reveal many details about how the attack unfolded, other than saying that 27 accounts were compromised and were then used to gain access to the portal and the data in question. The agency said the intrusion was detected on October 30, but did not offer any indication as to how long the attackers retained access to the grant portal. It also refused to rule out that names of applicants in "conflict areas and authoritarian states" may have been included in the stolen data – it is not known if recipients would have also been registered users – and said it is approaching the matter "very seriously." The grant portal, managed by Norad, which itself is part of Norway's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is responsible for handling applications from organizations across the world. Recent case studies include support for independent, investigative journalism in Moldova, a country which routinely battles Russian propaganda and election interference, and backing for Ukrainian children and prisoners of war. items.raw: Russia-linked group APT29 targeted iOS and Android users through hijacked websites and a compromised analytics service. Sekoia says a large-scale watering hole campaign is going after iOS and Android users, and it links the campaign to APT29 (aka SVR group , Cozy Bear , Nobelium , BlueBravo , Midnight Blizzard , and The Dukes ), the Russian group tied to the SVR foreign intelligence service. A watering hole is a site that attackers poison so visitors infect themselves. Sekoia found the campaign in mid-October 2026. It involved hacked or cloned high-profile websites in the US, Ukraine, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria. There’s also a supply-chain attack on a Ukrainian web analytics service, Plerdy, loaded by thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian. The attackers used three different methods to reach victims, but all led to the same malicious payload. They injected JavaScript into hacked websites, created fake websites that copied legitimate ones and secretly added malicious code, and compromised the Plerdy analytics service to infect websites using its script. Sekoia first spotted the campaign on the website of a Ukrainian gas production company. Other compromised sites included a major US chemical industry association, a European far-right political party and a Bulgarian website linked to the military. In the Bulgarian case, attackers modified an existing JavaScript library without changing the website’s visible pages. Researchers found no clear pattern in the targeted organizations, although they believe some websites may have been selected to reach specific individuals. Sekoia also identified two fake websites designed to impersonate legitimate services. items.summary: Kaspersky researchers analyze a complex fileless cyberattack by Storm-2603 involving ToolShell exploitation and subsequent runtime subversion, and discuss how to detect such intrusions.
items.raw: Executive summary In 2025, several threat actors exploited CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771 (ToolShell vulnerabilities) in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint to achieve remote code execution through crafted HTTP requests. One of the threat actors deployed ransomware on the target’s systems after successful exploitation. Microsoft attributed this ransomware-related ToolShell activity to Storm-2603, distinguishing it from other actors whose observed activity was primarily focused on credential theft, espionage, and data exfiltration. In December, our retrospective analysis identified activity consistent with Storm-2603’s TTPs. This activity involved the attacker using the IIS worker process as an in-memory bridge to the customer’s infrastructure, keeping the access and control layer entirely within w3wp.exe without writing anything to disk. Although subsequent post-exploitation activity generated disk artifacts, the bridge used to maintain access remained memory-resident. Let’s look in more detail at this attack. The attack chain, from reconnaissance to infrastructure compromise Intrusion timeline: Strategic latency and exploitation The intrusion analyzed in this report occurred in two stages, with a temporal gap between initial access and subsequent exploitation activity. The attack timeline was as follows: Dec 20 – Vulnerability fingerprinting: A single HTTP request targeted a SharePoint administrative endpoint associated with the ToolPane component to determine whether the host was vulnerable to CVE-2025-53770. Dec 21-23 – Tactical latency: A three-day period of silence followed the initial probe, separating the vulnerability fingerprinting from subsequent malicious activity and potentially reducing the likelihood of immediate detection. Dec 24 – High-intensity re-engagement: On Christmas Eve, when security staffing at many companies is reduced, the full RCE chain was executed through the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) on the same endpoint as the initial probe. Dec 26 – Incident discovery: The three-day gap initially prevented the December 20 probe from being correlated with subsequent malicious activity, marking the event as low priority. Retrospective analysis established that the probe was the initial phase of the subsequent intrusion. items.raw: Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability that attackers exploited to compromise 996 GS1900 network switches across 48 countries, exposing device configurations, network information and hashed root credentials. The attack began around August 17, according to cybersecurity firm GreyNoise, but researchers initially blamed a different vulnerability that Zyxel had already addressed. The newly identified flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-107441 , is a CVSS 8.8 out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the switches’ web management interface. It allows unauthenticated attackers with network access to execute operating system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests. The flaw affects ten GS1900 models, including GS1900-8, GS1900-24, and GS1900-48. Zyxel listed firmware versions ending in .2C0 and earlier as vulnerable, with model-specific fixes in versions ending in .3C0. Zyxel released a fix for CVE-2026-7273 in June, addressing a separate buffer overflow in the same switch series. GreyNoise initially attributed the attacks to that vulnerability, prompting CISA to add it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in September. However, security researchers at Binary discovered an exploit targeting a previously unknown flaw that remained effective even on switches running the June updates. The researchers reported the vulnerability to Zyxel on September 29. The attackers used a script to collect device configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. Such data can give intruders a useful map of an organization’s network and potentially help them move deeper into its infrastructure. Zyxel released firmware updates on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3. Administrators should update affected GS1900 switches, including those already running June security fixes.

items.title: BTCPay: ataque em servidor de criptomoedas resulta em furto de US$ 1,6 milhão
items.summary: Falha em servidor de criptomoedas resulta em furto de US$ 1,6 milhão
items.raw: A exploração de uma falha de segurança em servidores desatualizados do BTCPay Server resultou no furto de aproximadamente US$ 1,63 milhão em Bitcoin e Litecoin, conforme revelou uma análise publicada nesta segunda-feira (3) pela empresa de inteligência blockchain Bitquery. Os ataques ocorreram entre os dias 20 de outubro e 2 de novembro e visaram instâncias da plataforma de pagamentos que operavam com a versão 2.4.1 ou anteriores. A equipe do BTCPay Server destacou, em publicação feita no blog oficial, que a brecha explorada pelos cibercriminosos utilizou um método diferente para burlar uma vulnerabilidade que já havia sido corrigida no início de agosto. “Servidores desatualizados deixam fundos expostos a qualquer invasor que obtenha acesso administrativo”, afirmou a equipe do projeto, em comunicado oficial sobre o incidente. O caso evidenciou os riscos associados ao uso de “carteiras quentes”, que mantêm as chaves privadas armazenadas diretamente no servidor para permitir pagamentos automáticos sem a necessidade de assinaturas manuais a cada transação. Conforme destacou o BTCPay Server , a falta de manutenção e o atraso na instalação de pacotes de correção criaram brechas críticas que permitiram a invasão de instâncias desatualizadas. A Bitquery detalhou que a maior parte dos recursos subtraídos foi movimentada em poucas horas enquanto os servidores continuavam operando sem os devidos patches de segurança (correções de software para eliminar vulnerabilidades). A empresa de análise blockchain ressaltou que a prevenção existe rigor técnico constante: “Muitos operadores negligenciam atualizações básicas e mantêm ativos operacionais vulneráveis ao alcance de invasores“, destacou a equipe de pesquisa. Lições de segurança inspiradas em ocorrências na Binance Em paralelo, o incidente reforça debates sobre protocolos de proteção de custódia que também cercam gigantes globais do setor, a exemplo de ocorrências passadas de segurança e tentativas de invasão registradas na Binance . Analistas da Bitquery afirmam que o denominador comum em incidentes de grande escala envolve a exploração de pontos cegos em integrações de APIs e falhas na autenticação multifator. Ao passo em que a BTCPay Server recomendou a migração imediata para servidores novos com outras sementes de recuperação, o episódio serve como um alerta severo para empresas e custodiantes de criptoativo sobre a necessidade de isolar fundos operacionais e adotar autenticação multifator rigorosa em todos os nív

items.raw: Pull up your SOC’s compromised account playbook and read through the first 15 minutes. Most SOCs begin their response by calling or messaging the user via Teams to ask whether the 2:00 am sign-in from an unfamiliar country was indeed them. Their subsequent actions depend upon what the user responds with. Try that with a service account, and you’ll be waiting a long time. The same goes for an API key buried in a build pipeline, or an OAuth token somebody granted to a SaaS integration back in 2022 and hasn’t thought about since. Once one of those is stolen, your analysts are running a script that was written with people in mind, and the cracks tend to show well before the first shift handover. There are also far more of them than most boards realise. CyberArk’s research puts machine identities at roughly 82 for every human identity . Very few sit behind MFA, and a fair number hold far more access than the job they were built for. I’d add a problem that gets less airtime, which is that their traffic lives in the background noise your monitoring was tuned to filter out. Where the human playbook stalls Ownership is usually the first thing to slow you down. When a person’s account is compromised, HR can tell you who they are and who their manager is before you’ve finished your coffee. A service account pulling data it shouldn’t comes with no such shortcut, so the analyst burns the first hour working out which team built it. More often than anyone likes to admit, that trail ends at a contractor who left the business a year earlier. Say you do find an owner; containment still isn’t the clean step it is for a person. Lock a user out and one employee loses an afternoon. Pull a credential that a payments integration depends on, though, and you might take a customer-facing service down, which no analyst wants on their name at 11 p.m. without sign-off. So, they go hunting for somebody senior enough to approve the outage while the attacker carries on. Detection is the part people underestimate. An attacker with a valid token makes authenticated calls to the same endpoints the integration hits every day, and a patient one will even keep to its usual hours. Your impossible-travel rules were built around people moving between cities, so they have nothing to compare against here. Figure 1: One alert split into two paths. Ashish Mishra What recent breaches show Cloudflare’s write-up of its Thanksgiving 2023 security incident is worth a quarter of an hour of any CISO’s time.

items.raw: U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Apple flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added an Apple flaw, tracked as CVE-2024-27834 (CVSS score of 5.5), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog . “This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.” reads the advisory by CISA. CVE-2024-27834 is a security vulnerability affecting Apple’s operating systems and Safari. It could allow an attacker who already has arbitrary read and write capabilities on a device to bypass Pointer Authentication (PAC), a hardware-based security mechanism designed to protect memory addresses and prevent certain types of memory-corruption attacks. Pointer Authentication is a security feature implemented in Apple processors. It adds cryptographic signatures to pointers, helping ensure that memory addresses have not been maliciously modified. An attacker who gains the ability to read and write arbitrary memory could potentially exploit CVE-2024-27834 to circumvent these protections. This could weaken an important security barrier and make further exploitation of the device easier. What is the impact? Bypassing Pointer Authentication protections. Weakening defenses against memory-corruption attacks. Potentially facilitating further exploitation when combined with other vulnerabilities. Apple addressed the vulnerability through improved security checks in: Safari 17.5 iOS 16.7.8 and iOS 17.5 iPadOS 16.7.8 and iPadOS 17.5 macOS Sonoma 14.5 tvOS 17.5 watchOS 10.5 Cybersecurity firm Sekoia reports on attacks attributed with moderate to high confidence to Russia-linked cyberespionage group APT29. Attackers used compromised websites, fake websites and a supply-chain compromise of Plerdy SEO Tracker to deliver malicious JavaScript. The zero-click exploit chain targeted Safari and Chrome vulnerabilities to bypass security protections and deploy information-stealing malware capable of collecting browser cookies and device data. “Achieving arbitrary read/write access within the renderer is no longer sufficient for full exploitation on modern Apple silicon. This architecture relies on Pointer Authentication Codes (PAC) to cryptographically sign control-flow pointers. items.raw: A Canadian man was extradited to the U.S. to face charges over hacking universities and hijacking their computers to mine cryptocurrency. A Canadian man, Ryan James Roach (35), has been extradicted to the United States to face charges tied to a hacking operation that targeted universities and other schools. Roach was extradited on October 28 and now faces federal charges alongside Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, of Ontario. The indictment alleges that, from June 2016 to December 2019, the two men hacked computers, stole login details, and used victims’ machines to mine cryptocurrency for themselves. “They used virtual private servers in multiple countries, which were registered under false names. These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials.” DoJ states . “Victims of the scheme included educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts. Some of the computers damaged by the defendants were located at an institution of higher learning in the Western District of New York.” The targets were not random home PCs. Prosecutors say the pair went after U.S. schools with supercomputers, including institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina and Massachusetts. Some affected computers belonged to a higher-education institution in western New York. “To carry out the scheme, Roach and Stubbings surreptitiously accessed victim computers without authorization, deployed malware to gain control, stole victim login credentials, exfiltrated the data to servers that they controlled, and forcing victim computers to use their processing power to mine cryptocurrency for the financial benefit of the defendants.” DoJ continues. That is a lot of effort to turn someone else’s research hardware into a personal crypto rig. The alleged method was also more involved than a single phishing email. The indictment says they looked for weaknesses in victims’ networks, used servers and compromised machines from one victim to hide their tracks, and then moved through the network once inside. The duo used sophisticated techniques and tools to conduct reconnaissance and expand their access within the network. The charges include conspiracy to obtain information from and damage protected computers, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional damage to a protected computer. items.raw: AI agents help Joe Sandbox uncover malicious behavior concealed by evasion techniques and unmet execution conditions. Joe Security ‘s Adaptive Detonation brings active intervention to malware analysis, helping security teams investigate threats that may conceal their behavior during an initial sandbox run. Adaptive Detonation uses AI agents to examine execution results, identify obstacles preventing a sample from revealing relevant behavior, and select targeted interventions. These can include patching a blocking check, creating required files or settings, adjusting the execution environment, or supplying missing command-line arguments. Joe Sandbox then analyzes the sample again under the modified conditions to verify whether the intervention reveals additional activity. The approach addresses obstacles including keyboard restrictions, timing checks, firmware-based rejection, date requirements, and missing dependencies. By connecting observed evidence with targeted action and verification, Adaptive Detonation helps analysts investigate why a sample remains inactive and uncover behavior that might otherwise stay hidden. For security teams, this means deeper visibility into evasive threats and more evidence to support investigations. Adaptive Detonation is available as part of Joe Sandbox AI, a plugin for Joe Sandbox Cloud. Security teams can test Joe Sandbox by signing in or registering for Joe Sandbox Cloud Basic , the free community version. Read the Adaptive Detonation blog post for technical details, malware case studies, and original and follow-up analysis reports. About Joe Security Joe Security is a privately owned Swiss software company founded in 2011 and headquartered in Reinach, Switzerland. It develops malware and phishing analysis technology, combining dynamic analysis, agentic reverse engineering and dedicated analyst lab environments. Contact VP Marius Fitigau info@joesecurity.org

items.raw: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President ( AS2650 ). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period. The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica , a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications . Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge. There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer. Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight. Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network . “This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote . “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests

items.raw: The kinks in the software supply chain are once again being exposed, with attackers now targeting OpsShield’s update process. This week, threat actors used compromised credentials to push malicious updates out to cPGuard customers. They then accessed data stored on the vendor’s servers and in its billing portal accounts, and made copies of at least three of OpsShield’s cloud servers. The company said in an advisory that it has “shut the attacker out of every system we know they reached, and … are rebuilding the ones we cannot fully trust.” It has also released updates and urges customers to update to the latest version of cPGuard, change passwords, and generate new SSH keys. Ultimately, the breadth of this unsanctioned access underscores the continued fragility of the software supply chain, as well as the vulnerability of security tools themselves. “The real danger here is that attackers were able to turn a trusted security update mechanism into a vector to break into servers,” said Erik Avakian , a technical counselor at Infotech. “The software that’s supposed to protect those servers became the source that compromised them.” The anatomy of the attack OpsShield specializes in server protection and web security software. Its cPGuard product is a security suite, malware scanner, and firewall designed for Linux web hosting servers. The company disclosed that, between November 1 and 2, attackers were able to gain unauthorized access to the OpsShield update distribution infrastructure, and, for about 70 minutes, pushed out a malicious update. The threat actors began by probing OpsShield’s billing portal, registering a customer account under a false identity, and ordering a free cPGuard trial. They then sent crafted requests that allowed them to gain the ability to run commands on the server to collect data. They used stolen access keys to publish fake updates that ran as root (the highest level of admin privilege), and to copy sensitive files and make copies of three OpsShield cloud servers. About 2,950 customer servers ran the fake update, exposing password hashes, root SSH keys, MySQL root passwords, and shell history, OpsShield reported. Attackers also accessed about 7,900 billing portal accounts containing customer names, addresses, emails, and hashed passwords. items.title: Hackers também invadiram sistema de refrigeração de sangue na França
items.summary: Hackers invadem sistema de refrigeração e elevam temperatura de fornecedora de sangue na França
items.raw: Um ataque cibernético atingiu a empresa Coolworld, fornecedora de sistemas de refrigeração do Etablissement Français du Sang (EFS), o serviço de sangue da França. Na virada deste domingo (1°) para segunda-feira (2), cibercriminosos invadiram o software monitoramento remoto e alteraram a temperatura de câmeras frias usadas para armazenar amostras e plasma na região de Bourgogne-Franche-Comté. Os equipamentos costumam operar a 30° negativos e, na ocasião, registrou marcas de até 110°. A falha gerou alerta imediata após um técnico de plantão notar a alteração anormal nos termômetros durante a madrugada. A atuação rápida evitou danos operacionais e garantiu a transferência segura dos insumos para outras unidades. O semanário francês Le Canard Enchaîné revelou o caso no dia seguinte ao incidente. Hackers invadem sistema de refrigeração e elevam temperatura de fornecedora de sangue na França Foto: Divulgação/Grail O Ministério da Saúde da França informou que o incidente não causou consequências práticas e destacou que a situação foi controlada há tempo: O presidente do EFS, Frédéric Pacoud, explicou à imprensa local que a reação rápida da equipe impediu prejuízos: “Nós poderíamos ter perdido amostras ou bolsas de plasma destinadas ao tratamento de pacientes, mas a resposta evitou qualquer compromisso com a segurança dos produtos sanguíneos”. A instituição declarou já ter acionado a Agência Nacional de Segurança de Sistemas de informação da França para investigar a invasão. Resposta do fornecedor e contexto europeu A Coolworld confirmou, por meio de nota oficial , que tomou conhecimento do problema e implementou medidas de proteção. A empresa holandesa afirmou que a falha explorada pelos criminosos envolve um componente fornecido por terceiros : “A vulnerabilidade mencionada na mídia diz respeito a um componente fornecido por um terceiro não controlado diretamente pela Coolworld.”, destacou a empresa, no comunicado. O ataque ocorre em meio uma onda de incidente digitais voltadas contra sistemas de refrigeração na Europa. Há algumas semanas, redes de supermercados na França sofreram invasões em controladores de temperatura semelhantes. Outras nações registraram casos semelhantes nesta segunda-feira. Esse movimento levou a preocupação de autoridades de segurança sobre a vulnerabilidade de infraestrutura conectadas à internet. items.title: Ataques em massa miram repositórios no GitHub; 61 atingidos em 1 hora
items.summary: Ataque usa fonte falsa para roubar dados no GitHub
items.raw: Uma campanha coordenada de ataques cibernéticos atingiu 61 repositórios públicos no GitHub em menos de uma hora. A descoberta foi feita por pesquisadores da empresa de segurança Radware, que identificaram pelo menos 83 investidas contra projetos amplamente utilizados por milhares de organizações em todo o mundo . A maior parte das ações maliciosas ocorreu durante um intervalo de 43 minutos no dia 1° de setembro. De acordo com o levantamento divulgado pelo veículo The Register nesta quinta-feira (29), 67 itens maliciosos foram publicados durante o período, e outros seis surgiram logo depois. Como funcionava a estratégia dos invasores O método adotado pelos criminosos chamou a atenção dos pesquisadores pela novidade e pela automação. Os atacantes publicavam problemas, solicitações de extração ou comentários contendo comandos maliciosos escondidos em marcações de comentários em HTML, o que impedia que o conteúdo ficasse visível na página principal. As equipes de desenvolvimento precisam redobrar os cuidados com a segurança dos fluxos de automação. Para Babo, os desenvolvedores devem tratar conteúdos externos como fontes não confiáveis e restringir o acesso a segredos e variáveis sensíveis. Em contrapartida, Gabi Nakibly concluiu que a única forma de defesa consiste em garantir que o código dos fluxos de trabalho seja resistente e imune a esse tipo de falha. Siga o TecMundo no X , Instagram , Facebook e YouTube e assine a nossa newsletter para receber as principais notícias e análises diretamente no seu e-mail.

items.title: Gerador de energia residencial: como funciona e quando usar
items.summary: O gerador elétrico deve ser instalado em áreas externas.
items.raw: As quedas prolongadas de eletricidade podem representar grandes prejuízos, desde a perda de alimentos à queima de eletrônicos, bem como comprometer o uso de medicamentos, o acesso à internet e o abastecimento de água. Para reduzir os riscos, vale considerar investir em um gerador de energia residencial. Essencial para quem mora em áreas com apagões constantes , tempestades, fornecimento instável ou possui equipamentos que não podem ficar muito tempo desligados, o gerador produz eletricidade para uso doméstico enquanto a rede convencional estiver indisponível . Dessa forma, o usuário segue sua rotina normalmente. Há diferentes tipos de geradores e é importante conhecer cada versão para escolher a mais adequada. Saiba, a seguir, quais sãos os principais modelos e como usá-los com segurança. Como funciona um gerador de energia residencial? O gerador para casa é um dispositivo capaz de converter energia mecânica em energia elétrica , suprindo as necessidades energéticas caso a rede principal apresente falhas. Ele está disponível em vários tamanhos e tipos, e deve ser instalado na área externa da residência. Quando conectado ao painel elétrico do imóvel, o equipamento é acionado automaticamente assim que ocorre a queda de energia . A partir daí, passa a fornecer eletricidade para toda a casa, alimentando vários aparelhos e sistemas, no modelo fixo. A versão portátil, por sua vez, precisa ser acionada manualmente e exige a conexão dos aparelhos que receberão a eletricidade gerada. Esse modelo possui potência menor e geralmente é usado para dispositivos essenciais . O que acontece quando falta energia na residência? No caso do gerador reserva, como também é conhecida a versão para toda a casa, o sistema começa a operar segundos depois que a energia convencional cair . Esse modelo possui uma Chave de Transferência Automática (ATS) que monitora o fluxo da rede em tempo real, detectando a queda. Em seguida, a ATS coloca o motor da unidade geradora para funcionar, gerando energia a partir da queima do combustível . Como o sistema está conectado ao painel elétrico, a eletricidade produzida é distribuída por todo o imóvel com segurança ou pelos sistemas priorizados na instalação. Durante o funcionamento do gerador elétrico, a rede convencional fica desconectada da casa para evitar incidentes . Assim que a concessionária restabelecer o serviço, a tecnologia alterna para a rede, desligando o gerador, levando a interrupções mínimas. Apagões e quedas frequentes de energia

items.title: Recorteiro: a Rust banking trojan that cuts holes in your screen and hides behind fake electricity bills in Portugal
items.summary: TL;DR Fake “EnergiaLusa” electricity bills are infecting Windows users in Portugal with Recorteiro, a new banking trojan written from scratch in Rust. Its signature trick is to cut a hole... O conteúdo Recorteiro: a Rust banking trojan that cuts holes in your screen and hides behind fake electricity bills in Portugal aparece primeiro em Segurança Informática .
items.raw: We analyzed a campaign targeting Portugal that uses fake electricity invoices to install Recorteiro (also known by its operators’ names, “WindowsHelpers” and “CryptoPRO-X”). TL;DR Fake “EnergiaLusa” electricity bills are infecting Windows users in Portugal with Recorteiro , a new banking trojan written from scratch in Rust. Its signature trick is to cut a hole in a fake full-screen overlay , so the victim types a bank code into the real banking page while a human operator drives the session live over WebRTC. It also steals passwords, cookies, cards and crypto wallets. Every install has a unique hash, and the list of targets is pushed by the server. In our lab that list included Millennium bcp, Novo Banco, Santander and BPI . The operators are always watching: when a victim opens a targeted bank or exchange, the malware alerts the C2 instantly and the panel plays an alert sound, so an operator can jump in and monitor the session in real time . The kit is built for affiliates (at least four IDs found) and shows strong signs of Brazilian origin. Three panels, one business: a delivery console with tokenized links and an anti-Defender test desk (LoaderWeb), the CryptoPRO-X operations room, and a separate Android banking-fraud console (CyberControle). Introduction We analysed a campaign targeting Portugal that uses fake electricity invoices to install Recorteiro (also known by its operators’ names, “WindowsHelpers” and “CryptoPRO-X”). This banking trojan was written from scratch in Rust and is built to serve multiple affiliates: we found at least four distinct affiliate IDs across its builds . It combines fraud screens, live remote control and an operator who hand-picks which victims to attack. Portugal has been a steady target for Latin American banking malware for years, and we have followed several of these threats on this blog: Lampion (December 2019) spread through emails that imitated the Portuguese tax authority. Later waves used other trusted brands. Grandoreiro (May 2020) added Portuguese banks to its target list and gained new C2 features. Javali (February 2021) abused a legitimate Avira antivirus component to load its payload. Anubis (November 2020) was a phishing operation aimed at Brazilian and Portuguese users. A central back office drove many front-end phishing servers through a sync server. items.title: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
items.summary: Researchers say group may have been Kremlin-sponsored in search of diplomatic targets.
items.raw: Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday. The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data. Wielding DarkSword One of the impersonated sites was america250.org, belonging to a non-partisan group of lawmakers, business executives, and at least one former member of the Trump administration. The attackers registered america250[.]holiday and used it as a reverse proxy to america250.org. The imposter website delivered content from the real one that added malicious JavaScript into it. items.title: Apple turns iCloud into spy cloud, will start looking at public share links
items.summary: Content shared with anyone who has the URL will be scanned for 'harmful content,' though the iMaker hasn't defined that term
items.raw: If you share content using public iCloud links, Apple could soon be looking over your shoulder and checking for "harmful content." The iBiz announced plans to moderate publicly accessible iCloud share links in version 27.3 of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS on a support page published on Tuesday. To clarify, this applies only to iCloud content shared via links created to be accessible to anyone, as opposed to content shared directly with other people. “Items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content,” Apple explained on the new help page without bothering to define what harmful content means. Based on the wording, it appears those checks will apply to all iCloud items shared using "Anyone with the Link," which Apple says it can also access. The company hasn't explained how the checks will work. The share-with-anyone option removes end-to-end encryption from the shared item, Apple said, even if Advanced Data Protection, Apple's optional end-to-end encryption feature for supported iCloud data, remains enabled for the account. “If you try to upload harmful content, Apple reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time,” the help page continues, adding that the iMaker may also block or disable accounts associated with harmful content. The company also said it reserves the right to involve law enforcement when necessary, suggesting that its undefined "harmful content" category could include child sexual abuse material (CSAM), malware, and other potentially unlawful content. Without a proper definition of what it defines as harmful, however, iCloud users are essentially left at Apple’s mercy: If it chooses to continue to bend the knee to the Trump administration, for example, content deemed objectionable by the standards of political figures could end up wiped out. Apple also hasn't explained whether human moderators, automated systems, or both will be responsible for identifying and removing so-called harmful content, or whether any decisions will be left to AI, which can easily be fooled into making a bad moderation call. The scanning of such content, as mentioned above, begins with version 27.3 of Apple’s various OSes, which were released to developers in beta on Tuesday, with a general release expected in December. Apple didn’t respond to questions for this story. ®

items.title: Operação criminosa atinge mais de 40 instituições financeiras no Brasil
items.summary: Operação Open Ledger afeta mais de 40 instituições financeiras no Brasil
items.raw: Uma investigação de inteligência de ameaças divulgada pela empresa ZenoX revelou um esquema de comprometimento em cascata que afetou pelo menos 40 instituições financeiras e órgãos no Brasil . A operação, batizada de “Open Ledger” e conduzida por um grupo autodenominado “RedScanner”, utilizou agentes de inteligência artificial (IA) comercial para automatizar ataques e gerenciar infraestruturas de invasão. O relatório técnico foi compartilhado com exclusividade ao TecMundo , que agora apura mais detalhes sobre as empresas envolvidas. O esquema veio à tona após uma falha operacional na infraestrutura central dos criminosos, que mantinha um servidor com listagem de diretórios aberta e sem proteção na internet. O material coletado pelos analistas reuniu mais de 7 mil arquivos, incluindo transcrições de sessões de IA, ferramentas de comando e dados exfiltrados. Operação Open Ledger afeta mais de 40 instituições financeiras no Brasil Foto: Reprodução/ChatGPT O servidor comprometido era um nó Hetzner (empresa germânica de hospedagem de servidores e computação em nuvem) em Nuremberg, na Alemanha, e operava um serviço Python esquecido no diretório raiz sem autenticação ou criptografia TLS. Inteligência artificial como força de trabalho ofensiva O diferencial da operação foi o uso intensivo de agentes de inteligência artificial para conduzir o planejamento e a execução de tarefas técnicas de forma automatizada. De acordo com o documento técnico da ZenoX, o grupo manteve centenas de sessões transcritas e milhares de eventos automatizados rodando 24 horas por dia. “O RedScanner não usa IA como auxílio pontual: um agente de código comercial opera como força de trabalho primária da organização, com contabilidade própria no orçamento, rodízio automatizado de contas, LLM alternativa self-hosted para elasticidade, automação ofensiva 24 horas por dia e memória institucional mantida pela própria IA”, aponta o relatório da ZenoX. Para burlar restrições de segurança dos modelos de linguagem, os operadores utilizaram instruções sistemáticas para anular travas de recusa . Essa ação permitiu que a IA gerasse códigos maliciosos e gerenciasse rotinas de varredura sem intervenção humana constante. Estrutura organizacial do grupo RedScanner. O painel interno mapeia a divisão de papéis entre o administrador central (Janeth/Velhote) e os operadores humanos encarregados das execuções táticas. items.raw: Barracuda patched two flaws that can be chained to give attackers root access to Email Security Gateway appliances. Barracuda has patched two vulnerabilities that can be chained to gain root access to its Email Security Gateway (ESG) appliances. CVE-2026-116606 (CVSS score of 9.3) is an authentication bypass that lets unauthenticated attackers modify appliance configurations. CVE-2026-111560 (CVSS score of 8.6) is a command injection flaw affecting six Barracuda products. An attacker with administrator privileges could exploit it to execute operating system commands as root. “Barracuda has identified two vulnerabilities affecting certain Barracuda products: a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability and a command injection vulnerability. The vulnerabilities have been assigned CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 , respectively.” states the advisory . “Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product. If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device.” Barracuda quickly began fixing the problem and released security patches for affected products. Customers should check the affected products and follow the remediation guidance, make sure their systems use the latest firmware, and install all security patches. It has released patches and urges customers to update their systems, below are the affected products: Email Security Gateway (ESG) — affected by both vulnerabilities; patch with BNSF-40425 for version 9.4.017 or later , or BNSF-40430 for versions below 9.4.017 . Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC) — affected by CVE-2026-111560; patch with BNADC-16586 . Message Archiver (BMA) — affected by CVE-2026-111560; patch with BNMA-32468 . WAF Control Center (WCC) — affected by CVE-2026-111560; patch with BNWF-60060 . Web Application Firewall (WAF) — affected by CVE-2026-111560; patch with BNADC-16586 . Web Security Gateway (WSG) — affected by CVE-2026-111560; patch with BNYF-24789 . The vendor recommends that customers: Restrict administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks and use network access controls to reduce exposure. Check that devices are running the latest firmware and that all security patches are installed. If a device is several versions behind, install updates step by step; more than one update may be needed. Contact Barracuda Support if help is required.

items.title: Officials extradite Canadian man to US for alleged cryptomining spree
items.summary: Ryan Roach and his alleged co-conspirator, Mathiew Stubbings, are accused of compromising U.S. universities’ computers and taking over processing power to mine for cryptocurrency.
items.raw: Two Canadian men broke into the networks of multiple U.S. universities, stole credentials and implanted malware on compromised computers to commandeer processing power for a cryptocurrency mining operation , the Justice Department said. Ryan James Roach and Mathiew James Stubbings allegedly compromised the networks of at least four universities in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina and Massachusetts between mid 2016 and late 2019, according to an unsealed indictment. Roach, a 35-year-old from Saskatchewan, Canada, was extradited to the United States on Oct. 28 and arraigned Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of New York. Prosecutors said they are still seeking the extradition of Stubbings, a 41-year-old from Ontario, Canada. A grand jury previously indicted the Canadian nationals in April 2022. The men are charged with multiple cybercrimes and face up to 10 years in prison and up to a $250,000 fine, if convicted. Prosecutors accuse the men of researching and identifying potential victims with supercomputers containing vulnerabilities they could exploit. The men breached networks and deployed malware on compromised machines to take over systems, officials said. Roach and Stubbings allegedly rented virtual private servers based in Europe and the United States under false identities to conceal traffic, deploy rootkits, steal credentials and data, and transmit cryptocurrency mining software to compromised computers. “The defendants caused at least one supercomputer to mine cryptocurrency on their behalf, which caused much of the supercomputer’s processing speed and power to become unavailable to its legitimate owner,” prosecutors wrote in the indictment. Officials didn’t say how much cryptocurrency the pair allegedly mined for financial gain as part of the conspiracy. If convicted, Roach and Stubbings are also ordered to forfeit an assortment of networking and data storage devices, and any property or proceeds obtained through the alleged crime spree.

items.title: Operadoras terão que bloquear SMS não cadastrados para frear golpes
items.summary: Golpistas usam a engenharia social para roubar dados de acesso e enviar mensagens fraudulentas
items.raw: A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) publicou uma série de novas medidas para apertar o cerco contra golpes digitais via SMS no Diário Oficial da União nesta quarta-feira (04). As operadoras de telefonia móvel serão obrigadas a bloquear automaticamente mensagens corporativas de remetentes não cadastrados, assim como implementar um diretório público para rastrear a origem desses disparos. O motivo para essas alterações está relacionado a uma tentativa de frear o crescimento de fraudes que usam a tecnologia do SMS. Criminosos utilizam esse tipo de canal para aplicar golpes de phishing e, consequentemente, roubar dados. A nova regulamentação busca minimizar e rastrear essa prática. Um dos pontos alinhados tem relação com os códigos curtos, do termo short codes, em inglês. Eles constituem de cinco a seis dígitos e agora cada um deles será exclusivo de uma única empresa , com objetivo de acabar com o compartilhamento indiscriminado dessas numerações. A exceção fica para questões de operabilidade técnica. O grande destaque fica para a criação de um diretório setorial centralizado , que ficará disponível para consulta pública. A Anatel deu o prazo de 90 dias para que todas as pessoas jurídicas responsáveis pelo disparo de mensagens SMS, na modalidade Application-to-Person (A2P), sejam identificadas na plataforma. Segundo a determinação, a regra criada pela Agência indica que as operadoras precisarão impedir a entrega de qualquer SMS aos usuários se a mensagem for originada por um código curto que não esteja cadastrado na central. Essas empresas também precisarão realizar campanhas de conscientização para ensinar o consumidor a utilizar a nova ferramenta. Companhias terão 60 dias para implementar outros mecanismos O Despacho Decisório também informa que todas as operadoras deverão implementar mecanismos automatizados de monitoramento de tráfego em até 60 dias. Neste caso, o foco é fazer com que as redes identifiquem em tempo real certos padrões anômalos, campanhas de falsificação de identidade e uso de credenciais vazadas. Essas empresas vão precisar criar um canal de comunicação compartilhado para emitir alertas rápidos sobre incidentes de segurança; Companhias que usam o SMS para recuperação de senhas e a autenticação de dois fatores (2FA) terão que adotar procedimentos mais rigorosos para verificação de identidade dos usuários; A Superintendência Executiva da Anatel acompanhará as mudanças de perto e terá 180 dias para enviar um relatório ao Conselho

items.raw: Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration monitoring systems at three French blood banks, amid similar attacks targeting European supermarkets. A cyberattack has hit three regional blood banks in France, disrupting systems used to monitor and control refrigerated storage facilities. The incident took place overnight between Sunday and Monday, at roughly the same time hackers were targeting supermarket refrigeration systems across several European countries. The attack is particularly concerning because it targeted infrastructure that plays a direct role in protecting public health. Blood products must remain within specific temperature ranges to preserve their quality and ensure they’re safe for medical use. A disruption to refrigeration systems can therefore have consequences that go well beyond a conventional IT outage. According to the French Health Ministry, the incident affected several facilities operated by the French Blood Establishment (EFS). “Several regional facilities ​of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity ⁠incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems,” ​the health ministry said in a statement. “The incident had no impact on blood supplies,” Reuters reported , quoting EFS spokesperson Charley Dubois. Staff working around the clock received alerts about the problems and moved blood products to refrigerators that weren’t connected to the affected systems. This response helped prevent the incident from disrupting blood supplies, demonstrating how important operational procedures and contingency plans are when technology fails. “The situation was under control on Wednesday,” the French Health Ministry said, according to Reuters, which also reported that remote access to the affected refrigerators had been disabled. Investigations are now underway to establish how the attackers gained access, which equipment was affected and when the systems can safely return to normal operation. The timing is also significant. The French blood bank incident coincided with attacks against supermarket refrigeration systems in eight European countries, including Sweden and Belgium. Those attacks forced retailers to discard large quantities of food after hackers interfered with cooling and freezer systems. Instead, it sends you to app offers through affiliate tracking links. The page is not affiliated with Apple. If you’ve landed on a page like this, close it. The fake page promises $750 in Apple Cash Why Apple makes such good bait Apple is one of the world’s most recognized brands, and scammers use that familiarity to make fake offers seem credible. Apple’s own scam guidance lists fake promotions offering free products and prizes among common tricks. Current Apple news gives scammers useful cover. The new iPhone Duo is in the headlines, and we recently found a fake preorder page whose code tried to exploit older iPhones as soon as the page opened. With the iPhone Duo starting at $1,999, a promise of $750 in Apple money may catch people’s attention. The word “verify” may also sound timely. Starting November 9, Green Dot Bank, which issues Apple Cash, will require some users to verify their identity before they can reload their balance. A fake page asking people to “verify your device” to get Apple Cash may seem more plausible in that context. items.title: mSecure tells users to change passwords but won’t say why
items.summary: mSecure has urged users to protect information stored in its app, but hasn’t explained what happened or whether anyone’s data was exposed.
items.raw: Password manager mSecure has warned current and former customers to protect the confidential information stored in its app after detecting “suspicious activity.” But its advice about what users should do comes without an explanation of what happened or whose information might be at risk. The warning leaves users to decide whether to replace credentials—and whether it’s safe to store replacements in mSecure. While those are perfectly reasonable questions, mSecure’s warning does not answer them. In an email published by The Hacker News and sent to customers on November 3, mSecure’s developer, mSeven Software, said: “mSeven Software (‘mSeven’) recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application. In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist.” The notice recommends that customers “immediately take steps to protect all confidential information” stored in mSecure. Those steps: “may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys.” But the notice does not identify the suspicious activity, when it occurred, which systems were involved, or whether anyone accessed customers’ stored information . The Register , which also reviewed the email, noted that the company had not explained whether customers’ secrets were exposed. How to be safe Because the scope of the incident is unknown, we recommend prioritizing your most important accounts while mSeven investigates. Changing your mSecure password alone may not be enough if someone has already accessed your account. mSecure’s documentation explicitly warns that someone may already have made a backup of its contents. That guidance does not establish what happened in this incident. Users should not have to wait for a completed forensic investigation before receiving useful guidance. They need to know who should act, which credentials need attention, and whether the tool they would normally use to manage those changes remains safe to use. Until mSeven provides those answers, our advice is to prioritize your most important accounts, replace the relevant credentials through official services, and avoid destructive account resets: Change passwords through each service’s official website or app, beginning with your primary email, financial accounts, work accounts, and accounts used to recover access to other services.

items.raw: Exciting news for AI governance! Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider. What is ISO/IEC 42001? ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean? Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle. This certification means an accredited third party has audited our AIMS and confirmed that it aligns to the standard. To note, this isn’t a one-time exercise, as the certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits. This means our AI governance program is held to the standard for as long as the certificate is active. Why is ISO/IEC 42001 certification important? AI is continually evolving how security teams work, and it’s also causing teams to reconsider the questions they ask their vendors. Where does the model come from? What data does it use? Who reviews its outputs? How do we maintain the integrity and quality of our AI products? ISO/IEC 42001 certification gives customers independent evidence that Rapid7 has a management system in place to address those questions. It demonstrates that the in-scope AI systems are developed and operated under a structured program covering risk assessment, transparency, human oversight, and accountability. It also supports customers in their own governance work. Many organizations are building AI risk into their third party risk programs and preparing for frameworks and regulations such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. A vendor's certified AIMS doesn't replace a customer's own due diligence, but it provides a credible, audited starting point. As with cloud security, AI follows a shared responsibility model . Rapid7 is certified in the role of an AI provider, meaning we’re accountable for how we design, build, and operate these AI systems. items.title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist

items.raw: The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday. The heist, which both the FBI and the TRM Security firm attributed to North Korean actors, initially targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance wallets. The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum. Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page. The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft. Advanced persistent threat Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer's laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets. Like just about every organization that suffers a public, high-consequence hack, Binance said the threat actor was sophisticated and resourceful. Read full article Comments

items.title: US gov IT worker pleads guilty to sending Top Secret files to Ethiopia
items.summary: Help desk technician agrees to minimum 10-year jail term after being caught copying files for more than 2 years
items.raw: He swore an allegiance to the US, but he was working for someone else. An IT specialist who worked across US government departments and held Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to transmitting sensitive documents to Ethiopia. Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, admitted to the espionage offenses and agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months, the Justice Department confirmed on Tuesday. A naturalized citizen of the US, Lemma, of Maryland, had worked for the US government in different capacities and across different teams, including for the National Reconnaissance Office, State Department (DoS), and Justice Department (DoJ), between 2019 and 2023. These roles included working evening hours as an IT help desk technician at the DoS as of 2021, and daytime work at the DoJ as a contract management analyst, according to court documents. Lemma had what's known as "downdraft" authority, which is to say that he was permitted to move classified files between classified systems, and unclassified files from classified to unclassified systems. Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) – a secure workplace built for handling classified files. The criminal complaint [PDF] initially stated that the alleged offending began in July 2022, although the DoJ more recently claimed that it began in 2021. It claims Lemma was caught trawling "several" non-DoS classified portals and accessed intelligence reports without the proper authorization to do so. On various occasions, Lemma, who had held Top Secret security clearance since 2020, copied information from at least 133 intelligence reports without need-to-know authorization, according to court documents. Prosecutors claimed that the man downloaded more than 100 documents, burned them to CD/DVDs, and deleted their classification markings. The material Lemma was copying was at the Secret and Top Secret levels, but burned onto discs with green labels, which are approved for employees and are supposed to signify the contents of the discs relating to unclassified material only. Lemma would allegedly take these discs at the end of his shift and exit the SCIF with them tucked into his jacket pocket. items.raw: Introduction to BOD 26-04 On June 10, 2026, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk." Strip away the regulatory language and it reads like a single operational fact: for a vulnerability that is actively exploited, publicly reachable, and grants an attacker full control, you now have three calendar days to remediate it — and you must run a forensic investigation in parallel to determine whether you've already been breached. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, down from 38% the year before. That's a 43-day reality vs. a 3-day mandate; a gap you don't exactly just close by hiring more workers. This blog aims to break down what BOD 26-04 actually requires, mapping each point to the Rapid7 capability that helps to make compliance operationally achievable for all. What did CISA actually change? BOD 26-04 supersedes and revokes two prior directives: BOD 19-02 (2019), which prioritized internet-facing vulnerabilities by static CVSS score, and BOD 22-01 (2021), which created the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog but applied a 14-day patch deadline to every entry regardless of context. Note that flat timeline: under BOD 22-01, an actively exploited bug on an air-gapped internal server carried the same 14-day urgency as one on a public-facing web server granting full admin control. Teams burned cycles patching low-risk systems to satisfy a checklist. BOD 26-04 replaces that with a dynamic model: prioritize what attackers are actually exploiting, and formally defer what they aren't. The four variables to BOD 26-04 BOD 26-04 abandons CVSS as the sole trigger and evaluates every vulnerability against four binary variables, derived from the SSVC decision framework (CMU CERT/CC and CISA): Asset Exposure: Is the asset reachable by untrusted entities over a public network? KEV Status: Is the CVE on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog? Exploit Automation: Can an attacker automate the full exploit chain, enabling mass exploitation? Technical Impact: Does successful exploitation grant Total control (arbitrary code execution, full/admin privileges) or only Partial control (limited access, information exposure, denial of service)? items.title: VerifiedIDA | Making LLM-Driven Reverse Engineering Inspectable, Continuable and Reusable
items.summary: LLM reverse engineering scales only if analysis stays inspectable. A new standard and its open-source IDA Pro implementation tie annotations to evidence.
items.raw: Executive Summary SentinelLABS evaluated how frontier models reverse engineer binaries and annotate disassembler databases, finding recurring problems with inaccurate labels and incomplete analysis. To improve performance, we developed and tested a standard for LLM-driven reverse engineering that keeps annotations tied to evidence, verifies database changes, preserves project state, and requires review of the model’s work. We open-sourced VerifiedIDA , a reference implementation that applies the standard to autonomous reverse engineering in IDA Pro. Despite the growing capabilities of new models, our research shows that scaling reverse engineering requires that the analysis they produce remain inspectable, continuable, and reusable by humans, other models, and downstream security workflows. Overview The use of large language models (LLMs) for reverse engineering creates the possibility of examining binaries at a scale and speed exceeding that of manual analysis. It also makes reverse engineering accessible to those without specialized expertise in the discipline. The combination of scale, speed, and accessibility introduces a major shift across multiple domains. In cybersecurity, for example, defenders can analyze larger volumes of malware in less time, while attackers can misuse the same capability to considerably accelerate and scale vulnerability research and exploit development, shortening the time to exploitation and increasing the volume of intrusions. As part of our broader innovation initiative for applying AI to automate and scale up defense workflows to keep up with an increasingly fast and widespread threat landscape, this work contributes to making LLM-driven reverse engineering inspectable, continuable, and reusable. These properties are important when reverse engineering output is used as part of cyber defense operations, such as incident response, detection development, or threat hunting, where analysts act on this output, share it with other stakeholders, and use it as input to other tools and workflows. This requires the ability to inspect the evidence behind an LLM's conclusions to verify them, have another analyst or model continue the work from where the LLM stopped, and reuse results coupled with the code and data they describe. To this end, we focus on LLM-driven reverse engineering whose output is an annotated disassembler database, such as an IDA Pro , Ghidra , or Binary Ninja database. items.raw: Users looking for cracked commercial software, free games, plugins, and unofficial utilities could be signing up for more than a free download. Microsoft has observed an evolving campaign that uses trojanized installers to turn the downloading Windows devices into money-making machines, consuming their computing resources and internet bandwidth without informed consent. The campaign uses fake download pages and Inno Setup-style installers to deliver multiple software packages during a single installation session, Microsoft said in a blog post. The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly. “Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms,” the company said , adding that its Defender XDR detects and blocks several payloads and behaviors related to the campaign. Fake installers used for real money The campaign begins with users downloading installers advertised as cracked software , games, activators, plugins, or unofficial utilities. Microsoft observed lures posing as products like Navicat Premium and FabFilter audio plugins, alongside gaming and utility downloads. The installers use an Inno Setup-style wrapper to stage temporary executables under Windows’ temporary directories. Numbered payloads subsequently execute and coordinate the delivery of additional software. Microsoft said the campaign features an offer-based delivery mechanism. The installer communicates with rotating infrastructure using HTTP callbacks containing parameters such as “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution”. These requests allow the campaign to track individual software offers, allowing multiple payloads to succeed or fail independently within the same installation session. The first monetization branch is WorldProxyPool, which installs proxyware to route third-party internet traffic through the victim’s device. It also creates SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updates. Another branch installs CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC), alongside components such as VirtualBox, to facilitate distributed computing. items.title: Chrome 157 fixes 213 security issues, including 7 critical flaws
items.summary: Your browser may not have updated itself yet. Here’s how to check your version and install the fix manually.
items.raw: On November 3, Google issued Chrome 157 to the stable channel for Windows, Mac and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks. Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.38 for Linux . It includes 213 security fixes, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by Google. Chrome for Android was also updated to 157.0.8103.38 . It will become available on Google Play over the coming days. How to update Chrome The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update. If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it. Chrome 157.0.8103.39 is up to date You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system . Technical details Some of the security fixes deserve a closer look. Google rates seven vulnerabilities in the update as Critical. One, a memory corruption flaw in ANGLE, affects Chrome for Android. It could potentially allow a remote attacker to run code outside the sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page. items.raw: With a notable rise in autonomous AI agents veering off-script inside corporate networks, CrowdStrike has launched an enterprise AI Kill Switch, giving security teams control to cut off and disable models when they go rogue . Integrated into its Falcon Guardian platform, this AI Kill Switch will provide security teams with the human control to terminate the agent at its root, where it runs, block it from launching again, and even cut off its enterprise network access. The launch comes as enterprises increasingly deploy autonomous AI agents that can access sensitive data and execute tasks with limited human oversight. “These agents can access sensitive data, execute commands and interact with business applications independently, meaning enterprises may become aware of harmful incidents only after they occur. Existing security tools protect endpoints, networks and identities but may not fully understand an agent’s instructions, reasoning, tool calls and subsequent actions,” said Soumen Mandal, principal analyst at Counterpoint Research. Inside CrowdStrike’s AI kill switch The AI Kill Switch has been built on Falcon Guardian, which has the capability to discover the AI agents running in the enterprise. It uses the Falcon sensor to track what an agent is instructed to do, what it communicates, and what it executes. First, the Falcon sensor can terminate the running agent at the gateway, ensuring the malicious or misbehaving agent does not keep running while teams investigate. CrowdStrike said endpoint termination is also planned and will be available soon. Next, using the Falcon Guardian policies, the kill switch will prevent the agent from launching again on the targeted host or group of hosts. Next, it will cut-off agent’s enterprise network access. The action can be initiated by an authorised administrator, with every action being recorded in an audit trail. “Solutions such as CrowdStrike’s AI Kill Switch give enterprises a way to intervene quickly when AI agents behave unexpectedly, are compromised, or are manipulated through malicious instructions or scripts. This provides an important safeguard, allowing organisations to contain potentially dangerous or unauthorised agent activity before it causes significant damage,” said Devroop Dhar, MD and co-founder at Primus Partners.
