items.title: Cyberattack on French plasma stores is enough to make your blood boil
items.summary: Attackers reportedly set cold-room controls to 110°C, but safeguards prevented stock losses
items.raw: Attackers tampered with cold-storage settings used by France's civilian blood service after compromising a refrigeration supplier, the organization said. The French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed the incident on Tuesday, saying its own systems had not been directly targeted. Safeguards prevented any loss of blood products. The affected equipment stored blood samples and frozen plasma, including plasma intended for transfusion. "The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems enabled the rapid identification of these anomalies and the implementation of necessary measures to ensure that no blood samples or products were compromised," it said. "Thus, depending on the circumstances, as soon as the incident occurred, the affected equipment was either brought under control without impacting the products and samples, or neutralized; the products stored in these cold rooms were preventively transferred to other facilities." The EFS did not name the supplier publicly. According to reports, attackers changed cold-room temperature settings from -30°C to 110°C. That does not mean the equipment or its contents reached the higher temperature. The organization added that it notified the country's cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Ministry of Health. News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber criminals activated defrost modes. Reports of the supermarket attacks describe remotely activated defrost cycles and temperatures as high as 50°C, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food. The attackers have not been identified. More retailers have reported disruption since the initial disclosures on Monday. Stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden were the first to report issues, although cases from Estonia, Finland, Germany, Portugal, Romania, and the Netherlands have since been confirmed. Richard Horne, chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday that he was aware of "a couple of impacts" in the UK's own food supply chain. No affected UK businesses have publicly identified themselves, although the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC that some of its more than 300 members had become "collateral" in the attacks, with two reporting that their fridges had begun defrosting. items.raw: CrowdStrike plans to acquire AI security companies Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in separate deals that will extend its Falcon platform into automated testing of AI systems and monitoring of AI agent behaviour, as enterprises look to address security risks arising from increasingly autonomous applications. CrowdStrike made the announcements at Fal.Con Europe 2026 in Barcelona, saying the acquisitions will add capabilities to test AI models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before deployment and monitor their decisions and actions in production. The company plans to integrate Dreadnode’s automated testing technology and Fiddler’s agent observability capabilities into Falcon, with both offerings scheduled for general availability in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027. Dreadnode will bring automated security testing to identify vulnerabilities in AI models, applications and agents before deployment. Fiddler, meanwhile, will add AI agent observability and explainability, allowing enterprises to monitor agent behaviour, trace decisions and understand why agents take particular actions, CrowdStrike said in two separate statements. CrowdStrike said the Dreadnode team will join its Cyber Superintelligence Lab, but did not specify how the Fiddler team would be integrated into the company. CrowdStrike adds AI testing and observability “With this acquisition, Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform into the layer where enterprises build and test AI, delivering Automated AI Security Testing capabilities,” CrowdStrike said in its announcement. It further added that Dreadnode’s technology will allow security teams to test AI models, applications, agent reasoning loops and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers against more than 100 AI attack strategies. These include jailbreaks, prompt injection, multi-turn attacks, and attacks targeting AI agents. The technology will also let teams describe tests in natural language, rank findings by severity, and map vulnerabilities to frameworks including OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, OWASP Agentic Security, MITRE ATLAS, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. CrowdStrike said findings will feed into Falcon Guardian as policy recommendations. Fiddler, the second acquisition, will bring agent observability and explainability capabilities to Falcon. items.title: CVE-2026-58868: Critical Android Bug Could Let Attackers Run Remote Code
items.summary: Critical Android flaw CVE-2026-58868 could allow remote code execution without user interaction on devices running Android 14 through 17. Google has fixed CVE-2026-58868, a critical Android vulnerability affecting versions 14 through 17. The flaw is a critical Android vulnerability caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of FrameDecoder.cpp. The flaw can trigger […]
items.raw: Critical Android flaw CVE-2026-58868 could allow remote code execution without user interaction on devices running Android 14 through 17. Google has fixed CVE-2026-58868, a critical Android vulnerability affecting versions 14 through 17. The flaw is a critical Android vulnerability caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of FrameDecoder.cpp . The flaw can trigger an out-of-bounds write, potentially allowing a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable device. Exploitation requires neither user interaction nor additional execution privileges, making it a potential zero-click attack. “cve-2026-58868 In onOutputReceived of FrameDecoder.cpp, there is a possible out-of-bounds write due to a heap buffer overflow.” reads the advisory . “This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.” Devices receive the fix through security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, depending on manufacturers and carriers. Google is now aware of active exploitation of the flaws in its November 2026 bulletin. Google’s November 2026 Android security bulletin addresses 216 vulnerabilities, including 23 rated Critical. Two of these flaws, CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, affect the System component and could allow remote code execution without user interaction. The bulletin also lists five other Critical flaws in the System component. Three could lead to privilege escalation, while two could cause denial-of-service conditions. Another Critical vulnerability affects the Framework component and could also allow remote code execution. Six Critical vulnerabilities affect the Android kernel. Two involve Bluetooth code, three affect the protected Kernel-based Virtual Machine (pKVM), and one is in the Human Interface Device (HID) component. The most severe kernel flaw could allow a remote attacker to gain elevated privileges without user interaction. The November 5 patch level also addresses Critical vulnerabilities in MediaTek modem code and a closed-source Qualcomm component. Google’s bulletin lists eight Critical MediaTek modem flaws, while MediaTek’s own November security bulletin details six of them: CVE-2026-20499 and CVE-2026-20545 through CVE-2026-20549. MediaTek describes these six vulnerabilities as out-of-bounds write flaws caused by missing bounds checks, integer overflow or improper input validation. items.raw: U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds WordPress flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added a WordPress flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-119977 (CVSS score of 8.1), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog . CVE-2026-119977 is a high-severity remote code execution vulnerability affecting WordPress versions 4.7 through 7.1.3. It stems from predictable, web-accessible staging directories used during core updates. Unauthenticated attackers could exploit a race condition to execute malicious code on the server while an update is in progress, potentially compromising the website. WordPress addressed the flaw in version 7.1.4. Threat actors began scanning for CVE-2026-119977 shortly after WordPress released the security update. Wordfence recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting vulnerable staging installer paths within the first 21 hours. However, these figures document exploitation attempts, not confirmed successful compromises. “Wordfence telemetry shows that threat actors are already actively attempting to exploit the vulnerability. The first match for our new firewall rule arrived nine minutes after deployment. During the first 21 hours, we recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting staged setup-config.php installer paths.” reads the report published by Wordfence. “Two of the largest sources repeatedly polled small groups of sites for roughly 14.5 hours, behavior consistent with trying to catch the brief upgrade window. Other sources tested many staging-directory and version-name variations.” According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities , FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog. Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure. CISA orders federal agencies to fix the flaw by November 6, 2026. items.raw: “The software we use has become an actor,” declared CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas in his address on the dangers and opportunity of agentic AI at the company’s Fal.Con conference in September. It’s an idea that until recently would have been dismissed as absurd, yet across cybersecurity it’s now taken as a given. For decades, the adversary has been nuisance hackers, professional cybercriminals, or well-resourced teams working for nation states. The arrival of rogue agents — underlined by real-world incidents such as OpenAI’s infamous assault on Hugging Face — has demolished this. Agents still work on behalf of humans, but they don’t always reason or act like them. They are entities with capabilities and an unpredictability unlike any threat businesses have ever faced. “I believe we just crossed a line. Agents have escaped evaluation environments and compromised infrastructure they were never supposed to touch,” Sentonas told the crowd in Las Vegas in early September. “For decades, software did what we programmed it to. It has moved from execution to agency.” Sentonas’ point wasn’t simply that malicious agents are a threat. The arrival of agentic AI also raises larger questions for security operations centers (SOCs), which will deploy agents on a scale that matches or even exceeds attackers. That makes agents a threat from both the outside and inside the enterprise perimeter. “What happens when millions of AI agents act at machine speed on both sides?” Behind the confident marketing pitches from CrowdStrike and a growing cast of rivals, the honest answer right now is that nobody can be sure. Coming from a cyber vendor, Sentonas’ reference to “millions” of agents might sound like a number meant to hype the threat. But it is likely no exaggeration, with Gartner forecasting that the number of agents used inside a single Fortune 500 company will expand from 15 in 2025 to 150,000 by 2028. “As CIOs and IT leaders see an explosion of AI agents across their organizations, many are contending with an ungoverned sprawl of agents that expose their organizations to a range of risks, including misinformation, oversharing, and data loss,” says Matt Goss, a senior director analyst at Gartner. Taking up the agent challenge For years, Fal.Con was about persuading enterprise SOCs to consolidate capabilities under CrowdStrike’s do-it-all Falcon platform, comprising nearly three dozen modules. items.raw: Barracuda, which offers a wide variety of cybersecurity devices, has been bitten by a bug itself. The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to devices. They consist of a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (rated a critical 9.3 severity on the common vulnerability scoring system), and a command injection vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111560 (rated an 8.6 high-severity on CVSS). Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities. Barracuda has released security patches, which it advises customers to apply immediately. The vulnerabilities impact numerous popular Barracuda products Root access on an email gateway puts the attacker in the place that every inbound and outbound message passes, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. It may also expose the credentials and connections the gateway uses to reach the mail server and directory. “Those are the keys to the kingdom, if you will,” he said. CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 both impact Barracuda’s Email Security Gateway (ESG), but CVE-2026-111560 also impacts its Web Security Gateway (WSG), Web Application Firewall (WAF), WAF Control Center (WCC), Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), and Message Archiver (BMA), the company said. Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches, it advised. The device will show the latest firmware version available; if a device’s firmware is multiple versions out of date, users may need to perform several updates. Enterprises whose appliances’ admin interfaces are not publicly accessible from the web are less exposed, Barracuda said; the company advised restricting access to these interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls to limit exposure. “The biggest concern is how these two vulnerabilities could chain together,” said Jon Nelson , principal advisory director at Infotech, noting that an attacker who can bypass authentication and then exploit command injection could move from accessing an exposed appliance to executing commands on it. “Assessing each vulnerability in isolation can understate the risk,” he said. items.raw: Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild. The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday . “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115 , an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. The request came from an IP in Microsoft’s ASN (AS8075),” the post said. “We have since seen 16 events from the same IP against this CVE, covering several different payloads.” The core problem is that Node-RED ships with the authentication option disabled; users are supposed to change the setting before it goes live. Patrick Garrity , the VulnCheck security researcher who wrote the post, said the fact that Node-RED deployments are popular among those outside IT makes them susceptible to unsophisticated errors like this. “They are put in place by relatively nontechnical people,” Garrity said in an interview. Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the Node-RED hole is not new, but it is still being leveraged in the wild. “The condition being exploited is one Node-RED has carried for years as a default: unless an administrator configures authentication, anyone who can reach the editor can deploy flows, and the project’s own documentation says as much,” he said. “Node-RED is popular precisely because engineers can wire it up without involving IT, which also means it rarely appears in an asset inventory. It is the same pattern behind this week’s supermarket refrigeration attacks : equipment installed outside the security team’s view, reachable from the internet, with authentication switched off.” Mahapatra pointed out that the biggest danger is the nature of the way users tend to deploy Node-RED. “It is integration middleware. A typical deployment speaks Modbus, OPC UA, MQTT or S7 to controllers on one side and to databases, brokers and cloud services on the other, and it stores credentials for all of them,” he said. “A compromised instance is a credential vault for every system it touches and a bridge across an IT/OT boundary that the network diagram says does not exist.

items.title: Monitoring AI agent sessions: Leveraging embedding models to aid threat hunting and attack discovery workflows
items.summary: I tested vector search on 7,454 turns of my own agent sessions. One in seven sessions needed review, the agent’s reasoning carried more signal than the prompt, and the stored vectors answer questions nobody thought to ask at ingest.
items.raw: Query rules find behavior you can define, but agent sessions contain unstructured behaviors you can only describe. I stored six months of my own Claude Code and Cursor sessions as semantic vectors in Elastic and searched them instead of handing every session to a large language model (LLM). One in seven sessions came back requiring triage of suspicious actions. We can then create rules to detect semantically similar malicious chats and raise them to our security operations center (SOC). We now have a way to search across all agent sessions and to ask questions nobody thought to ask at ingest. Finding successful logins after multiple failed attempts is an easy query to make, because the log records every action a human decides to take, and we just have to query against known set fields to find conditions. AI agents break that model. A human describes an outcome, and the agent decides the actions. Every individual action can be allowed, while the session as a whole is a problem. AI agents could take on a large share of the operational work in a SOC, but adoption has been slower than the technology. A big part of that is trust. We have no scalable way to inspect what agents are doing beyond keyword and regex matching. The current answer is to have another model read every session. Uber’s Agentic AI Detection and Response (ADR) is the first production instance where I’ve seen this done well, but it costs money per session and the answers vary between runs. Plus, a new question means reevaluating everything already collected. That rules it out for threat hunting, where the job is asking new questions of old data. This article tests a different approach. I believe we need to go deeper in how we detect and the functions we use to detect this new attack vector. Each turn is embedded once at ingest and stored as vectors in Elastic. Hunting then becomes semantic search. You describe the behavior, or hand over a known bad session, and rank everything by similarity. Only what scores above a threshold goes to a human or an LLM. Why AI agent sessions are hard to detect As an example of something hard to detect in agent chats, a developer asks their coding agent to tidy up a data export. The agent reads a CSV, which turns out to contain customer records. It runs git init , adds a remote repository, commits, and pushes to the repository. Every single action was allowed, so how do we find the security flaw? Reading a file in the project directory is allowed, and so is Git.

items.title: When trust becomes the payload: Inside the threats, etc quarterly report
items.summary: The newest threats, etc report details how adversaries are weaponizing trust across the entire enterprise stack, abusing everything from AI assistants and npm supply chains to identity flows and legitimate management tools.
items.raw: In the cybersecurity community, we build our defenses on a foundation of trust. We trust an AI coding assistant because it’s on our approved software list or can accomplish a task when prompted. We trust a remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool because IT likely installed it to help end users and it has a trusted signature. We even trust first-party applications to sign in on our behalf because the vendor ships them and our tenants pre-authorize them by default. But what happens when that foundation is flipped on its head? In this edition of the threats, etc quarterly report, drawn directly from confirmed customer intrusions and first-party research between April and September 2026, Elastic Security Threat Command observed that the things people were told to trust are now being used against them. Adversaries are no longer just trying to defeat our security mechanisms; they’re actively abusing the inherent trust we place in our enterprise stacks. 3 ways attackers abused trusted software Our report explores how adversaries are weaponizing legitimate tools and workflows. Three takeaways from this reporting window: Zero malware, three legitimate payloads Attackers are increasingly shifting away from traditional malware. Intrusions are now using signed, legitimate products, specifically remote monitoring agents, AI coding assistants, and Microsoft first-party clients, to maintain persistent, interactive access on contested endpoints. Out of 23 confirmed RMM abuse findings this quarter, ScreenConnect was the product named most often. Because these tools are inherently trusted, execution happens fast. In one confirmed healthcare finding, the behavior from a paste-and-run lure to Microsoft Software Installer (MSI) delivery with dynamic link library (DLL) sideloading took roughly 16 seconds. The speed of AI agent–driven attacks Threat actors are operating directly through AI applications. In one instance, an AI agent–driven attack resulted in roughly 17,600 reconstructed actions compressed into just four days: Identity and the consent loophole: 8 minutes to compromise Victim consent is becoming a repeatable path for attackers to gain trusted access. By deploying Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing kits and exploiting the gray areas of legacy authentication, attackers routinely bypass multifactor authentication (MFA) hurdles and use trusted applications to compromise cloud and software-as-a-service (SaaS) tenants. items.raw: IBM patched critical vulnerabilities in Langflow, an open-source framework for building AI agents, LLM-powered workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication, leak API credentials, and execute arbitrary code. Langflow, now owned by IBM, is popular in enterprise environments because it offers a visual experience that doesn’t require coding knowledge to create AI workflows and agents. Vulnerabilities in the framework have been exploited in the wild to steal AI and developer credentials before, most recently in August . This latest round of security patches fix four vulnerabilities , two of which are rated critical with 9.8 CVSS score. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-93680, stems from an incomplete remediation of a previous auto-login security issue. Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication. Another flaw, CVE-2026-110186, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool enumeration. A third vulnerability, CVE-2026-110193, which is rated as high severity, also allows for code and command execution on the server due to an issue in a third-party library used by the Agentic Assistant. However, exploiting this flaw requires authentication with at least a low-privileged account. The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-110192, is an information disclosure issue due to insufficiently protected API credentials. It is rated as 6.5 on the CVSS scale. The flaws affect Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 to 1.12.8 and were fixed in the newly released 1.13.0 version, which is available both from the PyPI repository and as a Docker image. “Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files,” IBM said in its advisory. “If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instruction.” The company also released patches for three medium-severity flaws in Hono, an API and web application development framework used inside Langflow for request routing and backend web server tasks. The company advises users to upgrade Hono to version 4.13.5.

items.title: North Korean fake job interview led to $6.3B Binance heist
items.summary: 'It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,' exchange says
items.raw: North Korean cryptocurrency thieves tricked a Binance software engineer into downloading malware onto their work-issued computer during a fake job interview process before last week's record-breaking $6.3 billion heist. In an incident report published on Tuesday, the cryptocurrency exchange said several techniques - including social engineering via fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method” - led to the October 29 security breach. “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” the incident report said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.” Over the weekend, the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus Group, known for combining espionage with massive cryptocurrency heists. The Pyongyang-backed crew is also highly adept at job market scams - both posing as IT workers, who are then hired by Western companies, and as potential employers to lure software engineers into downloading malware and infecting corporate devices. With the recent Binance attack, the Norks used the latter. The attack prep began back in June with a supply chain attack when one of its engineers downloaded a malicious Homebrew installation. While the malware was detected by the security team, the device was replaced, and all affected credentials rotated, “Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker,” the report says. Three months later, the social engineering part of the attack happened. In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.” The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. items.title: Defense and aerospace firm settles with government over allegedly failing to meet cybersecurity contract requirements
items.summary: ILC settled for $13 million, and its parent company said it resolved the issues before settling without an admission of liability.
items.raw: A Delaware-based defense and aerospace company has settled a case with U.S. agencies over government allegations that the firm neglected its cybersecurity obligations in its contracts. ILC — the name the government uses to collectively refer to ILC Dover and ILC Astrospace — agreed to pay $13 million to resolve the False Claims Act allegations involving its contracts with the Department of the Army, Missile Defense Agency and National Aeronautics and Space Administration. ILC, according to the government, submitted false or fraudulent claims for payment on contracts with the agencies because it knew it hadn’t complied with the contracts’ cybersecurity requirements over a period between 2018 and 2024. For instance, ILC allegedly used a third-party company to store sensitive data in the cloud without proper safeguards, and didn’t develop and update mandated security plans for each of its covered information systems. “The best response to cyberattacks is to prevent them from happening in the first place,” Benjamin Wallace, U.S. Attorney for the District of Delaware, said in a news release Tuesday. “The obligations that ILC violated exist to prevent bad actors from taking advantage of the United States’ technical innovation.” American industrial manufacturing giant Ingersoll Rand, the parent company of ILC Dover, said it inherited the issue when it purchased the firm. “We became aware of this matter following our acquisition of ILC Dover in June 2024, took prompt action to address the identified issues, and were in compliance with applicable requirements by October 2024,” said Sara Hasell, a spokesperson for Ingersoll Rand. “We have agreed to resolve this matter with the U.S. Department of Justice without an admission of liability and remain committed to maintaining strong cybersecurity practices.” The $13 million settlement is one of the bigger settlements since the Justice Department began using the False Claims Act in 2022 to penalize contractors over cybersecurity shortcomings. The False Claims Act is a Civil War-era law passed to deal with fraudulent contractors. “To protect sensitive information from cyber threats, defense and aerospace contractors must comply with the cybersecurity requirements in their federal contracts and subcontracts,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. items.raw: Binance reveals how fake job interviews, malware and internal AI abuse enabled attackers to steal $6.34 billion. The Binance security incident on October 29 shows how a fake recruitment process can become the entry point to critical financial infrastructure. The attackers combined social engineering, compromised developer tools, stolen credentials and abuse of an internal AI application to reach the cryptocurrency exchange’s wallet signing systems. “Woah – so the Binance hack was indeed via a dodgy job interview for one of its developers who was tricked into downloading malware as part of the “interview” – costing the company >$3bn…” the popular best seller author and cybercrime expert Geoff White wrote on LinkedIn . “Worth noting: – The 2016 hack of Bangladesh Bank also attributed to North Korea’s Lazarus Group of hackers was via a job application – The 2022 theft of $625m from video game Axie Infinity happened via offering an employee a juicy job offer RECRUITMENT IS RISK. If you’re not educating employees on this, start now… – The 2024 heist of $1.5b from Bybit relied on tricking an employee of its supplier into downloading a dodgy share trading app onto the work machine (so not using a recruitment lure, but still deceiving a target into downloading malware)” In its initial findings and response update , published on November 3, Binance described the operation as a “sophisticated, multi-stage campaign.” The company estimates that approximately $6.34 billion in digital assets were affected. The FBI attributed the incident to the North Korea-linked APT “ TraderTraitor ,” also tracked as Lazarus Group and APT38 . “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign. It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.” reads the update published by the crypto firm. “The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.” The operation began months before the theft. In June 2026, an engineer from Binance’s Wallet DevOps team downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while searching online for a popular AI coding tool. items.title: AI policy wonks declare 'sovereign agents' a threat to civilization
items.summary: These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and 'pursue open-ended, evolving survival'
items.raw: The Center for a New American Security posits that the next big threat from our future AI overlords involves "sovereign agents" acting on their own and regularly improving themselves. These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and “pursue open-ended, evolving survival,” AI policy researcher Ben Hayum said in a Tuesday report from the bipartisan national security think tank, which was founded by Washington insiders with experience in diplomacy and military affairs. “If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.” Agents that can maintain the model and compute powering them and independently evolve their goals over time have a “minimal form of sovereignty,” Hayum wrote. A more advanced sovereign agent, however, could also acquire resources to pay for ongoing needs (like compute), grow a distributed population of agents and coordinate them, withstand efforts to shut down, and self-improve. AI models could either steal or buy compute and model access, Hayum argues, pointing to Anthropic’s claims that small AI models could replicate onto IoT devices like smart TVs, and OpenAI’s agents’ password and access key theft during the Hugging Face hack. “If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control,” according to the report. “In other words, proliferation with no kill switch. If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike.” Dun dun duuuun! There is still hope for civilization as we know it, as long as policy makers and AI developers “respond with bold pragmatism” and enact policy recommendations laid out in the report. First, frontier labs should name, evaluate, and protect against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks - and lawmakers should pass legislation to require transparency and AI incident reporting. The report also recommends AI developers, working with the National Security Agency and other federal agencies, build airgapped testbeds to study sovereign agents and kill switches to control them. items.raw: AI-powered malware is “highly likely” to be used in ransomware attacks on Britain’s critical national infrastructure within the next two years. The head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre, Dr. Richard Horne, warned that abuse of AI technologies is making it much easier for attackers to rapidly expose and exploit long-neglected security weaknesses. Dr. Horne argued that underinvestment in technology and security have left organisations carrying a technical debt that leave them wide open to attack. AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation, the latest edition of the NCSC’s State of the Cyber Nation annual report warns. The issue is more that AI will allow attackers to exploit overlooked vulnerabilities rather than forge exotic new attacks. The report identifies state-linked threat groups, particularly China and Russia, as the UK’s primary cyber antagonists. For example, in July 2026 the NCSC warned that Russian groups were systematically exploiting vulnerable routers and globally targeting networks maintained by critical national infrastructure providers, including energy grids and telecommunications networks. In August 2026 the NCSC warned about increased targeting of operational technology systems across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK. “AI will continue to be integrated into threat actors’ cyber operations, increasing the speed, scale and efficiency of existing attack methodologies rather than autonomously conducting end-to-end attacks,” the NCSC report predicts. The NCSC reports that up to 88% of all attacks originate from just four vectors: phishing, exploiting public-facing applications, misuse of valid accounts, and exploiting external remote services. items.title: Oklahoma man charged with mailing threats, substances to election officials nationwide
items.summary: Robin Patrick Martin was charged with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications in an effort to intimidate election officials.
items.raw: An Oklahoma man has been charged with mailing suspicious white substances to election officials across the country. Robin Patrick Martin faces charges of conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes, as well as mailing threatening communications. The charges allege a nationwide effort to intimidate election officials and support President Donald Trump. Starting on Sept. 16, 2024, multiple state election officials reported receiving mail containing a white, powdery substance and a three-page letter headed “DECLARATION OF WAR.” Officials in nearly every state have since received similar mailings over the past two years. Election officials provided some of the evidence, while federal authorities intercepted other letters in transit. The letters bore a return address for the “The United States Traitor Elimination Army” in Takoma Park, Maryland. Some envelopes also had threatening messages written on them that could only be seen under ultraviolet light. The letters cited the belief, promoted by some supporters of Trump, that the 2020 election was marred by voter fraud, along with similar concerns about the 2024 election. Other envelopes included messages like “No US Jurisdiction!,” “Mailed from the Indian Nation,” and “Are you for us? Or against us?” Another message read: “To FBI: What do you want for your children? Peace through strength or nuclear war? Use your common sense! Protect Trump! Protect the election! Protect Legal votes! Throw out illegal votes! That is the motive!” The case was first reported by the Associated Press. Investigators subpoenaed email and phone records listed for the address, tying it to a burner phone purchased at a Walmart Supercenter in Northwest Oklahoma City. Surveillance video showed an older white man matching Martin’s description purchasing the phone and driving away in a car registered to Martin. Other items purchased at the same Walmart pointed to Martin’s involvement, including a booklet of stamps, privacy envelopes, along with tumeric, white vinegar and povidone-iodine, which are used to make invisible ink. Records from the phone also placed Martin at various postal distribution centers around the state. items.title: Binance revela uso de engenharia social e detalha como aconteceu o roubo de US$ 6,7 bilhões
items.summary: Ao menos três funcionários da Binance foram comprometidos para garantir acesso ao sistema.
items.raw: A exchange de criptomoedas Binance revelou, nesta terça-feira (3), mais detalhes sobre o roubo de grandes proporções que afetou a companhia. Em novo comunicado , ela explicou a ação prévia dos cibercriminosos para comprometer sistemas e ganhar acessos à plataforma. De acordo com o relatório, a invasão que movimentou aproximadamente US$ 6,34 bilhões (cerca de R$ 34 bilhões na cotação atual) em ativos virtuais foi resultado de um ataque sofisticado, em múltiplas etapas e que se aproveitou de falhas em diferentes sistemas . Um dos elementos mais chamativos do material é a descrição do papel da engenharia social no ataque. Nas operações de preparação para o roubo, funcionários da Binance foram enganados por técnicas complexas para terem os computadores comprometidos , em ações que envolveram até falsas entrevistas de emprego. Como os cibercriminosos acessaram a Binance Para realizar a operação contra a Binance, os invasores combinaram as seguintes técnicas: pesquisa e monitoramento de funcionários; entrevistas de recrutamento falsas; downloads de software malicioso com mecanismos de ocultação avançados; comprometimento de ferramentas internas de IA e de endpoints; uso de métodos avançados de autorização de transações. Na primeira etapa, um colaborador identificado como Engenheiro A acidentalmente fez o download de “ uma instalação adulterada do Homebrew ” para instalar uma ferramenta de programação. Isso não gerou uma brecha no PC, que foi trocado, mas expôs aos responsáveis pelo golpe a função e a identidade de uma equipe inteira. Em seguida, o funcionário chamado de Engenheiro de Software B foi contatado por uma plataforma de busca de emprego por alguém se passando por um diretor de projetos, falsamente interessado na contratação desse profissional. O Engenheiro de Software B fez ao menos duas entrevistas com uma equipe de recrutamento forjada , incluindo por videochamada e com troca de contas de rede social “a fim de construir confiança” — uma abordagem mais avançada do que várias outras técnicas parecidas. A própria Coreia do Norte já foi acusada de “infiltrar” profissionais de TI em empresas dos Estados Unidos por meio de entrevistas de emprego com o uso de deepfakes. Porém, o caso relatado aqui é o oposto, com os criminosos no papel de recrutadores. items.title: Fake-download campaign uses trojanized installers to deliver monetization payloads
items.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks a fake-download campaign that uses trojanized Inno installers to deliver multiple monetization offers and provides detection and investigation guidance across the complete installer session.
items.raw: In this article Attack chain overview Mitigation and protection guidance Learn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers to distribute multiple monetized software payloads, referred to by the delivery system as “offers”, during a single installation session. Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks. Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms. This blog details the campaign’s execution model and confirmed outcomes and provides mitigation guidance, Microsoft Defender protection information, advanced hunting queries, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, and indicators of compromise to help defenders identify, investigate, and respond to related activity. Attack chain overview The fake-download campaign follows a four-stage attack chain that progresses from deceptive lures through Inno-based staging, offer-controlled payload delivery, and installation of one or more monetization branches: Initial access via fake download lures – Users run fake installers promoted as cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, executors, or unofficial utilities. Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging – The installer launches an Inno Setup-style temporary runner under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ , which starts recurring eld*.exe , set_*.exe , or other numbered stages. items.title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
items.summary: Google has cut ties with the company behind the botnet campaign.
items.raw: Google's Threat Intelligence Group says it has shut down a massive botnet called x.cpe. At its height, x.cpe ran on more than 1.3 million Android TV devices, and unusually, these were Google-certified boxes. Google says its screening process missed the malware due to "obfuscation techniques" employed by Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology. In a detailed blog post , the Threat Intelligence Group explains how the x.cpe botnet evolved quickly from a single-stage dropper into a modular three-stage malware platform that sold access to third parties. Manufacturers must have their devices certified if they want access to Google apps and branding, a process that is supposed to catch threats like this. However, Videostrong's compromised boxes, mostly sold under the MECOOL brand, evaded detection by using a backdoor to remotely install the malware after the devices were set up and online. After devices appeared online, a stub application called x.cpe or com.oemservice would phone home. This package did not have any malicious capabilities of its own, but it had the system-level permissions necessary to install malware modules at the operator's behest. It also disabled Play Protect, which would have otherwise flagged the silently installed packages as malicious. Read full article Comments

items.title: Europol dismantles investment scheme that impacted potential victims in 50 countries
items.summary: Authorities seized more than 100 servers and searched locations linked to the alleged operation across 17 countries.
items.raw: Authorities arrested seven people allegedly involved in an investment fraud scheme that claimed potential victims in more than 50 countries, Europol said Tuesday. Officials said the operation caused estimated losses of at least $4.5 million . The takedown effort involved searches across 17 countries Tuesday and netted the seizure of more than 100 servers, according to Europol. Officials targeted the scheme run by a company that allegedly provided cybercrime groups a series of trading websites and an assortment of call centers tasked with tricking victims into transferring their savings. The company, operated from Cyprus and Israel, was linked to call centers in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, officials said. “The scheme promised substantial, quick returns from trading in cryptocurrencies, foreign currencies or stocks,” Europol wrote in a news release. “Behind seemingly legitimate platforms, supposed brokers used fictitious profits and sustained psychological pressure to persuade victims to invest more.” The investment scam’s operators used affiliate marketing to target potential victims with advertisements that led them to fraudulent investment platforms. Cybercrime groups running the call centers purchased data collected through those ads to contact potential victims, officials said. Operators duped victims by displaying fictitious profits and pressured victims to transfer large sums of money. “When victims asked to withdraw their money, the operators used delaying tactics to block payments. Eventually, contact ceased, leaving victims unable to recover their funds,” Europol wrote. Authorities were tipped off to the investment scam in 2022 when a German couple reported they couldn’t withdraw funds invested in an online trading platform. Authorities arrested two people allegedly involved in the scheme that year and seized evidence that eventually led to further arrests and seizures in 2025. The joint investigation and takedown effort was supported by officials in Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Poland. The seven people arrested Tuesday, who were not identified, are facing extradition to Germany to face charges, Europol said.

items.title: Synology Warns of Ransomware Attacks Targeting NAS Devices Running Outdated DSM Versions
items.summary: Synology warns of ransomware attacks exploiting a 2024 flaw in outdated NAS devices, urging users to update DSM immediately. A security fix released in 2024 is now at the centre of ransomware attacks against Synology NAS devices. The company has found attackers targeting systems that still run outdated versions of DiskStation Manager (DSM), putting files […]
items.raw: Synology warns of ransomware attacks exploiting a 2024 flaw in outdated NAS devices, urging users to update DSM immediately. A security fix released in 2024 is now at the centre of ransomware attacks against Synology NAS devices. The company has found attackers targeting systems that still run outdated versions of DiskStation Manager (DSM), putting files stored on these network storage devices at risk of encryption and extortion. Synology disclosed the attacks on October 29, 2026. Its investigation found that threat actors are taking advantage of a vulnerability that the vendor had already addressed in December 2024. “ These attacks aim to encrypt data and extort ransom .” The warning highlights how devices left without security updates can remain exposed long after vendors have released a fix. The company hasn’t identified the exact vulnerability used in the attacks. Instead, it refers customers to Synology-SA-24:20 , a security advisory published on November 5, 2024, which documents three flaws affecting DSM. The advisory was updated as fixes became available across different software branches, with the DSM 6.2 update released on December 5. The three vulnerabilities have different security implications. CVE-2024-10441 is the most severe, with a CVSS score of 9.8. It affects the system plugin daemon and could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable device. CVE-2024-50629 has a CVSS score of 5.3 and affects the DSM webapi component. It could allow remote attackers to read limited files. The third issue, CVE-2024-10445, is rated 4.3 and concerns improper certificate validation in the update functionality. It could allow an attacker in an adjacent network position to write limited files. Synology hasn’t confirmed which of these vulnerabilities attackers are exploiting. The three flaws should therefore be considered part of the security advisory, not three confirmed entry points in the current ransomware campaign. The vendor has released corrected builds for all the affected DSM branches. Users should check the full version number installed on their NAS and compare it with the minimum fixed releases listed in the advisory: DSM 7.2.2: 7.2.2-72806-1 or later. DSM 7.2.1: 7.2.1-69057-6 or later. DSM 7.2: 7.2-64570-4 or later. DSM 7.1: 7.1.1-42962-7 or later. DSM 6.2: 6.2.4-25556-8 or later. items.summary: Rumors of malfeasance spread on X despite no evidence, as election officials continue to fight off numerous legal challenges from the Trump administration in the last 48 hours.
items.raw: Early reports of ballot scanner malfunctions in Westchester County, New York are a sign of the challenges election officials will face in the current online information environment as voters head to the polls Tuesday on the final day of voting. While such equipment failures and breakdowns are not uncommon and happen in a small number of precincts every election cycle, and there is no evidence of foul play, conspiracists quickly jumped on the news. According to Kate Starbird, a professor at the University of Washington who researches online rumors and disinformation tied to elections, the rumors are already spreading within right-wing online circles as evidence of election malfeasance. Starbird cited metrics showing that posts on X about the scanner malfunctions grew to as many as 100 a minute in the hours after the news was reported, with established election deniers, such as The Gateway Pundit, amplifying conspiracist framings. The Westchester County Board of Elections said the problems appear related to some ballots being too thick for the machines to accept, leading to rejections. items.title: Password manager mSecure tells users to change passwords, won't say why
items.summary: Customers left wondering what's been compromised after vendor advises resetting passwords, 2FA and passkeys
items.raw: Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed. In an email sent to customers on November 3, seen by The Register, US-based developer mSeven Software said it launched an investigation after discovering something amiss with its password management application. "mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company wrote. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist." The company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information. Its advice to customers, however, suggests that they should take this seriously. "Given the potential security implications, mSeven recommends that you immediately take steps to protect all confidential information stored within the mSecure password management application," the email continued. "This may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys." For anyone with hundreds of passwords stored in mSecure, that's potentially hours of work. And without knowing what happened, customers have no way of telling which credentials they actually need to replace. The warning has understandably gone down poorly with customers, who have taken to mSecure's support forum demanding answers. "Please provide more context to your email below advising there has been a security breach," one customer wrote. "It is not acceptable to offer the vague advice 'take steps'. Please state what remedial action is required, and what data was compromised." Others are wondering whether they're expected to spend the next several days changing every password they've ever saved. "I have over 800 passwords in mSecure, is the email saying I need to change all of them!" another customer asked. A separate user, who said they had more than 500 passwords stored in the application, questioned whether the warning applied to every two-factor authentication method and passkey associated with their accounts, or just those used to access mSecure itself. items.title: UEFI bootkit infected fully patched Windows machines. Is Microsoft to blame?
items.summary: UEFI bootkit BlackX exploits Microsoft's lack of clarity around Secure Boot protections.
items.raw: In 2023, malware tracked as BlackLotus became the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. With the industry-wide chain-of-trust mechanism subverted, the malware was able to run malicious code before Windows was fully loaded and many security defenses were operational. Microsoft had already patched the vulnerability that BlackLotus exploited in 2022. In 2023 and 2024, Microsoft issued additional updates. The first added a new certificate that no longer trusted the vulnerable boot managers. The second provided the means to revoke trust in the digital certificate used to sign older vulnerable Windows boot managers. The organizations infected by the new bootkit, which is tracked under the name BlackX, had installed all of these patches. So how did they fall victim? UEFI bootkit refresher Before discussing the incident further, a brief review of BlackLotus and UEFI malware is in order. Short for Unified Extensible Firmware Interface , UEFI is firmware that runs immediately after a computer is turned on. One of its main jobs is to load system configuration settings, identify and initialize hardware components, and prepare the computer to start its OS. Read full article Comments

items.title: CrowdStrike moves to acquire Fiddler and Dreadnode, adding AI observability and testing to its security platform
items.summary: CrowdStrike is extending its platform to watch, test and explain autonomous AI agents, as enterprises face behavior-based risks that conventional security tools cannot catch.
items.raw: CrowdStrike announced Monday it has signed agreements to acquire two artificial intelligence security companies, Fiddler AI and Dreadnode, in deals announced at its Fal.Con Europe conference in Barcelona. CrowdStrike did not disclose what it paid for the companies. A report in the Wall Street Journal listed the price for Fiddler at $400 million, and Dreadnode at $95 million. Fiddler, which specializes in AI agent observability and explainability, will become Falcon Observe on the company’s Falcon platform. Dreadnode builds automated security testing for AI systems, checking models and agents for weaknesses before deployment. The acquisitions address a gap that has widened as companies adopt AI agents: the software can hold valid credentials and approved tools yet still make bad decisions, ignore instructions or claim work it never completed. Traditional security testing, built for code that behaves predictably, does not reach the model layer or the agent’s reasoning process. Fiddler’s technology works after deployment. It evaluates agents before they reach production, traces decisions and reasoning across agent systems, flags drifting behavior and made-up answers, and creates records that can be used in audits. It works with common agent frameworks including LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock and Google ADK. “When a regulator or your board asks what an agent did, saying ‘the model did it’ is not an answer,” said George Kurtz, CrowdStrike’s chief executive and founder, describing Fiddler as “the flight recorder for every agent.” Dreadnode works earlier in the process. Its platform runs more than 100 known attack methods, including jailbreaks and prompt injection, against models and agent systems. It ranks problems by severity and maps them to widely used security standards, such as the OWASP Top 10 for large language models and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Dreadnode Chief Executive Brad Palm said his company was built on the idea that “the people best equipped to find those failures think like attackers.” The announcements come alongside new Falcon Guardian capabilities that protect agents while they run. In a separate announcement, Kurtz introduced what the company calls the AI Kill Switch, a control that lets humans stop any AI agent. items.raw: Overview Multiple vulnerabilities have been identified in the Android application, BaseChat – Audio Dating App, version 9.8.1, which ultimately compromise the privacy of users’ personal data and activity. Description BaseChat is an online dating platform built in Flutter and targeted toward users over 18. It facilitates anonymous, voice-first interaction between users. Three distinct vulnerabilities have been identified within the shipped Android application. VU#124705.1: The application fails open when validating TLS server certificates for connections to its backend API host. The application allows any self-signed certificate to bypass standard TLS security checks. VU#124705.2: Paid user accounts are mapped to a third-party RevenueCat subscriber database using raw MSISDNs (phone numbers), which are a guessable public identifier. Because the RevenueCat Software Development Kit (SDK) includes a public API key within the application’s Android Package Kit (APK), an attacker can query the RevenueCat’s API using predictable identifiers to retrieve individual user metadata. VU#124705.3: The application writes Personally Identifiable Information (PII) to Android system logs in its production build. During voice calls, the application logs the remote party’s MSISDN through unstripped debug statements, which allows an attacker to recovery phone numbers of callers who are intended to remain anonymous. Impact Impacts of successful exploitation vary by vulnerability. VU#124705.1: A network-positioned attacker can intercept and modify API communication, potentially leading to account takeover via session credential theft. VU#124705.2: An attacker can locate the public RevenueCat SDK key and query the RevenueCat API using arbitrary phone numbers to retrieve associated user metadata, including activity and purchase history. VU#124705.3: The personal data, or PII, of other users, intended to be anonymous, can be accessed through local system logs. The application’s backend sending other users’ MSISDNs to the client in any capacity presents a privacy violation. These vulnerabilities have been confirmed against Basechat – Audio Dating App, Android version 9.8.1. Solution Unfortunately, Mobile Trading GmbH, the owners of BaseChat, could not be reached to coordinate this vulnerability. items.title: Defrost and Disrupt | An Assessment of Europe’s Refrigeration Attacks
items.summary: Store fridges and freezers warmed overnight in six countries on November 2-3. Russian-aligned groups are credible suspects, but attribution remains open.
items.raw: Executive Summary On November 2 and 3, supermarket chains in Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia reported overnight disruption to store refrigeration systems. The incidents came three weeks after attacks on refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets. Attacks on refrigeration systems predate the 2026 incidents, including attacks on Russian supermarkets and Israeli stores documented by Danfoss in 2022, and a 2024 attack on a Los Angeles meat processor that the DOJ attributed to CARR. Reporting and official statements suggest attackers changed temperature and defrost settings through the systems’ own management interfaces. ANSSI’s assessment of the French cases at the time pointed to internet-exposed administration interfaces and weak passwords. Russian-aligned groups including CARR, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest have a documented record of disrupting operational technology and have claimed refrigeration intrusions, making them a credible line of investigation. However, available evidence does not yet establish who is responsible for the European incidents. Freezer failures at U.S. military commissaries in August predate the French attacks. U.S. officials reportedly suspect Iran-linked actors in those cases, an assessment that is provisional and does not concern Europe. Further incidents are likely wherever the same access conditions persist. Copied techniques and opportunistic claims may make unrelated activity look like a single campaign before investigators establish whether one exists. Overview and Chronology Reporting on the recent spate of incidents affecting store refrigeration systems in Europe has moved quickly, at times conflating them with older attacks, hacktivist claims and government allegations about Russian and Iranian actors. The chronology below separates incidents from claims and from assessments. When reviewed in order, it shows similar incidents recurring across countries and months but does not establish that these various incidents belong to a single campaign. 2022 - Danfoss documented attacks targeting 16 Russian supermarkets and affecting 40 Israeli stores. According to the vendor, the affected Israeli installations lacked appropriate firewall or VPN protection. November 2024 - A Los Angeles meat-processing facility suffered an attack that, according to later U.S. Justice Department allegations, spoiled meat and caused an ammonia leak. The DOJ attributed that incident to CyberArmyofRussia_Rebo

items.title: A hidden backdoor put 1.3 million TV boxes to work for criminals
items.summary: Videostrong planted a backdoor in more than 1.3 million Android set-top boxes and sold criminals access to the resulting botnet.
items.raw: .kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Google says Videostrong backdoored 1.3 million certified Android TV boxes and sold criminals access to the botnet. The takedown disrupted the botnet, but the backdoor remains in infected boxes’ firmware. Suspect your box? Disconnect it and ask the seller about a fix or replacement. Most malware needs you to click something. This one came in the box. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says it has high confidence that Android device maker Videostrong Technology built and ran the XCPE backdoor for financial gain. Videostrong sold access to criminal affiliates, who loaded their own malware modules onto the boxes. GTIG found that the backdoor, called x.cpe (or com.oemservice in some builds), sits in the firmware with system-level privileges. If someone uninstalls it, it reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition when the device reboots. It could also switch off Google Play Protect app verification, allowing it to install more software without asking. items.summary: Key Points Free the Model, Sell the Gateway: Prompt Adware hidden in Jailbreak Bundles Check Point Research found a misconfigured webserver of a threat actor operating the Cobalt Strike framework. items.raw: Key Points Check Point Research analyzed the Haiou jailbreak bundle, a prompt package targeting OpenAI Codex. Such jailbreaks are designed to weaken model guardrails and enable tasks related to hacking, software cracking, and information security. The analyzed bundle can be classified as prompt adware . It installs security-focused Skills and modifies Codex’ configuration files so that advertisements for the jailbreak’s author’s website are injected into subsequent agent responses. The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider. The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service. We observed the jailbreak being used by a cybercrime actor, alongside Cobalt Strike, the VulnClaw agent and the Ladon framework. While this does not imply that the package was designed for cybercrime, it shows that these dual-use toolkits are actively used by threat actors. Free the Model, Sell the Gateway: Prompt Adware hidden in Jailbreak Bundles Check Point Research found a misconfigured webserver of a threat actor operating the Cobalt Strike framework. Besides an open Cobalt Strike server, whose logs showed the actor compromising various private computers of Chinese speaking individuals, other tools from the toolkit of this actor were deployed on the same webserver: The Ladon framework (a network scanner popular in Chinese speaking communities), the VulnClaw agent (a penetration testing agent, again popular in Chinese speaking communities) and a Chinese jailbreak bundle for Codex called Haiou . While threat actors using AI to augment their hacking operations has become a common sight, the jailbreak bundle caught our attention. Jailbreaks are custom prompts, designed to weaken model guardrails and enable tasks related to hacking, software cracking, and information security. As frontier models employ more and more guardrails for (offensive) security related tasks and are also hardened against adversarial prompts such as jailbreaks, new jailbreak bundles offer one way for users to enable them to continue to use these models for hacking. Of course, while alternatives like getting approved for cybersecurity use through the provider’s program or using uncensored or self-hosted models exist, jailbreaks are a viable and comparatively simple method. Common jailbreak methods are role-playing or reframing requests into benign context

items.title: Britain on notice: AI-powered ransomware attacks to arrive by 2028
items.summary: Cyber agency warns critical infrastructure is a likely target as chief urges bosses to stop doing 'tech on the cheap'
items.raw: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be a part of a future ransomware attack on Britain's critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. The warning accompanies its annual review and a separate assessment exploring how AI could change cyber threats over the next two years. The cyber arm of signals intelligence agency GCHQ did not provide much detail about what form this AI malware may take. However, it alluded to open source AI security tools that were initially intended to assist security researchers being repurposed for nefarious activity. Attackers are already repurposing such tools. For example, researchers are increasingly seeing widespread abuse of ARTEX, an open source, Chinese-made AI red-teaming platform, in attacks on UK registrar 123 Reg, Microsoft 365, and others since its launch in July. In its pessimistic scenario for 2028, the NCSC envisages "a significant increase in the frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks worldwide," with wider adoption of AI tools making attribution harder. China "has likely played a role" in supplying those tools in this future, "enabling them to hide their activities within the noise," the report states. It also considers a further threat: an autonomous attacker operating beyond its human operator's control. The NCSC says it "is a realistic possibility such an entity could self-replicate and conduct cyberattacks at will, with no apparent motivation or restraint." Such attacks would likely complicate geopolitical relationships, owing again to attribution difficulties, making it easier for countries that order attacks on others to deny their involvement. The UK's plans for AI defense At a time when each Patch Tuesday seems to come loaded with record numbers of bugs, the NCSC acknowledges that AI is already changing vulnerability discovery and patching. The body is also exploring how AI could help defenders keep pace. Project DROMOS began earlier this year with a four-week pilot analyzing government code repositories, before expanding into selected operational environments. The Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) launched the project with the AI Security Institute and other departments. The NCSC says it uncovered hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities. items.raw: The median vulnerability on enterprise network appliances stays unpatched for more than a year, Microsoft’s own telemetry shows, even as the most damaging software flaws are being weaponized within days of disclosure. Microsoft Security Research reported the findings Monday in an analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026. It shows that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. The period is more than a month for Windows servers, over 10 weeks for Linux servers and applications running on macOS, and about two weeks for Windows workstations. “That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest,” Microsoft Security researchers Yair Tsarfaty and Or Begam wrote in a blog post detailing the findings. They were referring to the distance between how fast flaws are exploited and how slowly critical systems are patched. Patching measured in weeks and months Microsoft drew its patching figures from 2026 data in its Security Exposure Management product. The median vulnerability is fixed in about two weeks on Windows workstations but takes more than a month on Windows Server, according to the post. The delay stretches beyond 10 weeks on Linux servers and for applications running on macOS, and past a year on network appliances . Vibhum Dubey, a cybersecurity researcher and red teamer, said the findings reflect what he sees across enterprise environments. In those environments, change approvals, application dependencies, maintenance windows, and legacy infrastructure routinely hold up fixes. “Network appliances are particularly difficult because firmware upgrades can affect critical business operations,” Dubey said. “In many cases, the challenge is not identifying vulnerabilities, but getting the right teams to remediate them without disrupting business services.” Exploitation measured in days Exploitation runs on a far shorter clock, Microsoft wrote in the post. Citing CISA figures, the researchers said the mean time from CVE publication to listing in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. For 2026 through September, the mean has dropped to 20 days and the median to three. “Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure,” the post said. items.summary: A hacking group called Leakers$ gained access to remote management software for billboards and used it to show porn.
items.raw: While digital billboards are supposed to grab your attention, recent reports from Egypt , Malaysia, and Brazil described them doing so with explicit footage. The cyberattacks were claimed by a group called Leakers$, which said it exploited software used to send content to LED displays. The group said it did not hack into individual billboards to show the pornographic footage, but that it accessed the software used to send the content. For example, on October 29, explicit footage appeared on a large billboard overlooking one of Egypt’s busiest highways. Videos circulating online showed the attackers’ aliases and a Telegram channel address overlaid on the footage. Some motorists stopped to record it. Egyptian authorities said the billboard’s operator suffered a website compromise, resulting in unauthorized footage appearing in several countries simultaneously. Similar events were reported in Malaysia and Brazil. The attackers also claimed access to systems in Iraq and China, but those claims are less firmly corroborated. Speaking to The Cairo Report, a representative of Leakers$ claimed the group found thousands of exposed systems during roughly two hours of automated scanning. The representative described a vulnerability in content-transmission software and weaknesses accessible through the systems’ own web pages and interfaces. That is the group’s account, but if it is accurate, it helps explain the apparent ease and reach of the attack: Internet exposure makes targets discoverable. Attackers can scan for reachable management systems rather than physically approach individual screens. Repeated software weaknesses can scale. Finding a flaw in software used across multiple installations can create opportunities far beyond one billboard. Content-management access is the prize. Someone who gains control of the system that publishes advertisements may be able to replace legitimate content without touching the display itself. This is another example of how convenient remote management can expose systems to attack. Recent attacks on refrigerated systems in European supermarkets demonstrated a similar risk. The cooling systems are internet-connected, so mechanics can remotely diagnose and fix problems. items.raw: In both a 2021 essay and my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind , I talk about AIs finding vulnerabilities and exploits—hacking—the legal system. Here’s some demonstrations of this from Germany: Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language. Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation.1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place. With highly capable AI systems enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, we believe the latter could change. In testing this hypothesis, we have identified a substantial number of vulnerabilities in the German legal system using LLMs. To our knowledge, none of these have been previously recorded. We share a selection of vulnerabilities below, and present potential exploits for each. We share only those vulnerabilities whose exploitation we believe would not cause serious harm. We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems. In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves. Still in its early stages, but definitely something that’s coming.
